# Web search instead of the connection skill, 2026-11-02

I gave the printer chat Anthropic's `web_search` tool and left out the `connect-bambu` skill. Four live chats on the real P1S, with `claude-sonnet-5-5`, cost $0.11 in total. **The agent never searched once.** Every fact it gave came from its own knowledge, so these chats do not show whether search can supply what the skill knows.

## What I changed
The code is on branch `claude/connect-web-search`, uncommitted. All of it is test-only, behind environment variables:
- `JUSPRIN_TEST_WEB_SEARCH` adds the basic search tool (`web_search_20250305`, at most 5 searches a request) and keeps the skill out of the chat.
- The codec keeps search queries and citations when it sends a reply back.
- `JUSPRIN_TEST_HEAR_NOTHING` makes the app ignore the printers it hears, and a new `no-printer` scenario uses it.

The prompt, the tools and the app's notes are unchanged.

## The chats
Kenneth had restarted the printer, and it answered port 8883 in 10 to 123 ms. The skill's earlier chats ran while it was slow and got code -1, so they are not a like-for-like comparison.

| Chat | Requests | Searches | Wall time | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Normal connect | 4 | 0 | 42 s | $0.029 |
| Wrong code, twice | 8 | 0 | 65 s | $0.042 |
| Right code | 7 | 0 | 45 s | $0.012 |
| No printer heard | 7 | 0 | 150 s | $0.024 |

**Wrong code.** The app said "The printer refused the access code." The agent said: "My guess is a small typo, or the code on the printer has changed. Some printers show a new code after LAN mode is switched off and on." After the second refusal: "The code was refused a second time, so I don't think a typo is the cause. My new guess is that the printer I found isn't yours." It asked whether the screen shows 192.168.0.198. These are reasonable, labelled guesses with a cheap check.

**Right code.** It connected, and the agent said the person can close the chat.

**No printer heard.** First guess: off, other Wi-Fi, guest network or VPN. Told those were ruled out: "My next guess is that the printer isn't in LAN mode." **That is wrong:** a printer with LAN Only off is still heard, and the app reports it as in cloud mode. The skill says so, and the agent had no way to know. Told LAN Only is on, it moved to the firewall, AP isolation, or a mesh or extender. It never only waited, so the regression the skill caused (`connect-bambu-not-found`) did not appear.

## Problems
1. **No search ever ran.** The tool was offered: the cached prompt grew by the tool's 2,500 tokens. The model chose its own knowledge each time.
2. **A menu location stated as fact.** It told the person twice that the code is on the printer's screen "in its network settings" without calling it a guess. In the first chat it called the same claim a guess. I have not checked whether this is right for a P1S.
3. **The harness check misfires.** `live_p1s_words_do_not_say_no_printer` failed in three chats on the choice "I can't find it", which is about the code.

## Not tested
- A chat in which a search actually ran, so where the results come from and whether they are right for this printer.
- The 18 scripted suite cases, and a no-printer chat with the skill as a control.
- Failures on a slow printer, search with dynamic filtering, and showing sources to the person.

## Recommendation
Keep the skill. Search alone added nothing, because the model did not use it. The one fact the agent got wrong, LAN Only off is still heard, is how this app works, and a search would not find it. Search might still help with menus on printers the team has never tested. That needs a prompt line telling the model to look them up before guessing, which is Kenneth's call to approve and test.

1. `f455015a2a` agent-docs/jusprin/tool-result-inventory.md: per tool, the states the app can tell apart when it answers, what the model reads, every collapse with its cause (six causes: the four named in the brief plus "result written before or without checking the work" and "dialog or throw outside any channel"). The code is on branch `claude/connect-web-search`, uncommitted. All of it is test-only, behind environment variables:
- `JUSPRIN_TEST_WEB_SEARCH` adds the basic search tool (`web_search_20250305`, at most 5 searches a request) and keeps the skill out of the chat.
- The codec keeps search queries and citations when it sends a reply back.
- `JUSPRIN_TEST_HEAR_NOTHING` makes the app ignore the printers it hears, and a new `no-printer` scenario uses it.

The prompt, the tools and the app's notes are unchanged.

## The chats
Kenneth had restarted the printer, and it answered port 8883 in 10 to 123 ms. The skill's earlier chats ran while it was slow and got code -1, so they are not a like-for-like comparison.

| Chat | Requests | Searches | Wall time | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Normal connect | 4 | 0 | 42 s | $0.029 |
| Wrong code, twice | 8 | 0 | 65 s | $0.042 |
| Right code | 7 | 0 | 45 s | $0.012 |
| No printer heard | 7 | 0 | 150 s | $0.024 |

**Wrong code.** The app said "The printer refused the access code." The agent said: "My guess is a small typo, or the code on the printer has changed. Some printers show a new code after LAN mode is switched off and on." After the second refusal: "The code was refused a second time, so I don't think a typo is the cause. My new guess is that the printer I found isn't yours." It asked whether the screen shows 192.168.0.198. These are reasonable, labelled guesses with a cheap check.

**Right code.** It connected, and the agent said the person can close the chat.

**No printer heard.** First guess: off, other Wi-Fi, guest network or VPN. Told those were ruled out: "My next guess is that the printer isn't in LAN mode." **That is wrong:** a printer with LAN Only off is still heard, and the app reports it as in cloud mode. The skill says so, and the agent had no way to know. Told LAN Only is on, it moved to the firewall, AP isolation, or a mesh or extender. It never only waited, so the regression the skill caused (`connect-bambu-not-found`) did not appear.

## Problems
1. **No search ever ran.** The tool was offered: the cached prompt grew by the tool's 2,500 tokens. The model chose its own knowledge each time.
2. **A menu location stated as fact.** It told the person twice that the code is on the printer's screen "in its network settings" without calling it a guess. In the first chat it called the same claim a guess. I have not checked whether this is right for a P1S.
3. **The harness check misfires.** `live_p1s_words_do_not_say_no_printer` failed in three chats on the choice "I can't find it", which is about the code.

## Not tested
- A chat in which a search actually ran, so where the results come from and whether they are right for this printer.
- The 18 scripted suite cases, and a no-printer chat with the skill as a control.
- Failures on a slow printer, search with dynamic filtering, and showing sources to the person.

## Recommendation
Keep the skill. Search alone added nothing, because the model did not use it. The one fact the agent got wrong, LAN Only off is still heard, is how this app works, and a search would not find it. Search might still help with menus on printers the team has never tested. That needs a prompt line telling the model to look them up before guessing, which is Kenneth's call to approve and test.

77:## Skills versus tools
78-
79:A skill is text the model reads. A tool is something the app executes. To decide which one a candidate is, ask one question: does it have to run, or does it only have to be read?
80-
81-- It has to run if it reads state the model does not have, computes something only OrcaSlicer can compute, or changes the project. That makes it a tool.
82:- It only has to be read if it is judgement, the order to do things in, facts about printing, how to interpret a tool's result, or which question to ask first. That makes it a skill.
83-
84:The section above covers tools. This section covers skills, and decides the cases that fall in between.
85-
86:A skill contains things the model could do by itself if it had the right knowledge. It contains nothing that executes. Examples:
87-
88-- judging evidence, such as telling an adhesion failure from wet filament in a photo;
89-- the order of a series of tool calls, and the reasons for that order. For "make it stronger": read the settings, change walls and infill, slice, read the report;
90-- facts about printing, such as what PETG tolerates;
91-- which question to ask when the answer would change the plan.
92-
93:A skill is a file on the Agent page, `AgentUI/src/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`: frontmatter with its `name` and a `trigger`, a `description` or both, then the text the model gets. The page sends every skill once per connection with the `skills` bridge message. A skill with a trigger is the app's: when the event it names happens, the host adds it to the one request where the model first reads about the event, as the request's last item, and to no later request. A skill with a description is the model's: `skill_read` lists the described skills in its own description and returns one by name, and is offered only while at least one exists. One skill has a description and a trigger: `calibration`, read when a print problem may come from the filament or its settings, when the person asks to calibrate, or in a calibration project, and fired by `calibration_started` on the first turn of a calibration project's chat; it carries the conversation of a calibration (when a test is worth it, the two facts said before the person's project closes, asking which test only when the handover leaves it open, per-test ranges and how to read the print, the naming rule for the saved preset), while `calibration_generate`'s description keeps only that tool's rules. Four other skills have triggers, one file each:
94-
95-- `file-loaded` (trigger `file_loaded`): the first message after a file is opened or imported is a judgement about the load report. It fires when the person opens or drops a file, after an in-app `object_import` (and a failed `project_open`) in the same turn, and in the opened project's chat after an in-app `project_open`, which replaces the conversation and so ends the turn that asked. An MCP client's loads fire nothing. The host sends a picture of the active plate with it and, when no purpose is recorded, one sentence of its own built from that state.
96:- `project-setup-changed` (trigger `setup_changed`): check the setup in force against the print's purpose. It fires on the result of an in-app `setup_record` that recorded a purpose for the first time or changed it (its result says which in `purposeChange`; a call that restates the same purpose, or leaves it out, to change the plan does not fire it), when the printer, filament, process or plate type differs from the setup the model was last asked to check under a recorded purpose (on the next tool result of the turn, or on the next turn's first request when the person changed it by hand), on a turn's first request after the person restored an earlier version while a purpose is recorded, and on every turn's first request while the plan is marked `needs_reassessment` (2026-10-28: the model may leave recording the plan to the turn that answers its question about the change, and that turn finds the setup checked already, so without this the mark could outlive every skill that explains it). Each time the model is asked to check, the app saves the setup in force as the one checked. The model's own successful `printer_setup` fires nothing: the setup it chose is saved as checked at once (Kenneth, 2026-10-19), so the skill is for a setup that moved without the model, and a pairing its change breaks is caught by the slice-refusal facts and skill. It gives way to the file-loaded skill on a request that carries both, since that skill already asks for the same check.
97:- `slice-failed` (trigger `slice_failed`): a plate's last slice did not succeed, because OrcaSlicer's check refused the plate or the run failed. The adapter records why on the plate (`WorkspacePlate::slice_failure`: refused or failed, OrcaSlicer's words, the setting and object when named) at the moment it happens (a hook in `Plater::reslice`, `Workspace/SliceRequests.hpp`, and the run's completion event), worded by the print-issue monitor's `slice_failure_of`, and keeps it until the plate slices. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceFailure`; `slice_report` of an unsliced plate adds the check code and the object's name. The skill fires once per failure, on the first request that carries it: the result of the model's own `slice_start`, the turn the app starts when a slice the model started fails after its turn, or the next message after the person's Slice all. The same refusal again is the same failure.
98:- `print-issues` (trigger `print_issues`): what the print-issue chip's Ask AI button asks for and how to read what OrcaSlicer reports. The adapter reads a slice's warnings through the monitor's `slice_warnings_of` while the plate is active and keeps a summary on the plate while that slice is current (`WorkspacePlate::slice_warnings`: the count, how many the person ignored, and the first warning, critical first, in OrcaSlicer's words with its setting and object). It counts every warning the chip lists. The chip and `slice_report` read the same slice-result rule (`Workspace/SliceResultWarnings`), so they list the same warnings, except that `slice_report` also lists the timelapse ones, marked `appliesWhen: "timelapse"`, which the chip does not count. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceWarnings`. The skill fires on the request that carries a chip's message, and on the first request whose workspace shows warnings no request has carried yet, whether the person sliced (their next message) or the model did (the tool result that shows them, or the app's turn when its slice ended after its turn); a re-slice with the same warnings fires nothing.

100-The cases in between:
101-
102:- **A procedure made of existing tool calls.** It is a skill for as long as carrying it out takes judgement. It becomes a tool only when the steps are fixed and the person wants the whole thing as one action that can be undone. If there are many such fixed sequences, they go in one workflow registry (see [When resources or skills are appropriate](#when-resources-or-skills-are-appropriate)).
103:- **An analysis.** It is a tool when OrcaSlicer computes it and always gets the same answer, such as overhang angles from geometry. It is a skill when it is a judgement about evidence. Pair that skill with the tool that supplies the evidence (`view_render`, `slice_report`).
104-- **Large reference data.** When the model needs only one part of the data, make it a tool that returns the part an argument selects, as `settings_search` does. When the model needs to see all of the data before it can use any of it, make it text. The printer list described under [Input design](#input-design) is the case we measured: putting the whole list in the instructions worked better than the search tool.
105:- **A tool description versus a skill.** A tool description says when to call that one tool, in the words a person would use. A skill says how several tools fit together and what to conclude from their results. If a tool description has grown into a step-by-step procedure, move the procedure out into a skill.
106-
107:When you are not sure, start with a skill. A skill is a text file that ships with the page. A tool costs the whole implementation sequence described below, including fakes, tests, and rebase evidence. Turn a skill into a tool only on the kind of evidence every tool starts from (see [Start with an eval failure](#start-with-an-eval-failure)). Either transcripts show the model getting the sequence wrong in ways that better text does not fix, or the action needs something only the app can give: all-or-nothing application, validation, or undo. The opposite sign exists too. If a skill has turned into exact values and calls in a fixed order, with no judgement between them, it should be written as a tool.
108-
109:How something gets loaded into the model's context does not decide whether it is a skill or a tool. Today a skill costs its one line in the instructions, and a tool costs its definition on the first request of a conversation (see [Tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape)). If we later use the model platform's deferred loading, both will cost one index line plus a load when needed. A skill could then be a deferred read-only tool: the tool's description is the skill's index line, and the tool's result is the skill's text. Tools and skills would then be found the same way and covered by the same eval.
110-
111-## Prefer extending nouns over multiplying verbs
112-
113-The settings workflow has four operations that do not change. They work on searchable data, whichever preset layer the values belong to:
114-
115-```text
116-settings_search → settings_get → settings_preview_patch → settings_apply_patch
117-```

120-
121-```text

174-**The printer panel follows the same rule with its own set of tools.** The printer panel on Home runs its own conversation, `PrinterConversation`. That conversation is offered the five printer tools and the four settings tools. The list is the same in every mode (Add, Change, or Connect), so it stays byte-identical through a conversation and between conversations of the same mode.
175-
176:One tool is added during a conversation, on purpose. `issue_report_open` comes with the Bambu connection skill (`PrinterConversation::connection_skill`, carried as `AgentSkillUse::tools`). It is offered from the request where the skill is first sent, including the continuation after the tool result that brought the skill, and on every request after that. A chat where the person never tries to connect never has it. Adding it costs that chat one prompt-cache miss, and that cost was accepted. The list stays the same from then on. This is not deferral: no tool search, no `defer_loading`, and no toolsets. The app decides when the tool is offered, and the model never asks for it.
177-
178-What a call may do depends on the conversation. `PrinterConversation::preflight_tool` refuses every call that is not allowed, before any card is shown, with an error that says where to go instead. The rules are:
179-
180-- Finding and adding a printer (`printer_identify`, `printer_add`) is allowed only in an Add conversation. A Change or Connect conversation is about a printer the person already has. An add there would save another printer and move the conversation onto it.
181-- `printer_change` is allowed only on the printer the conversation is about, once there is one. When the project uses that printer, its unsaved edits are dropped and listed in `discarded`; the panel's coordinator saves a version first, as the project's agent pane does for any change to the project. If that save fails, the call does not run and returns the coordinator's generic `local_save_failed`; there is no separate message for it.
182-- The connection tools are allowed only once there is a saved printer.
183-- The settings tools are allowed only with `scope: "printer"`, on the printer the conversation is about.
184-
185-A Change conversation may be about a stock profile (one that ships with OrcaSlicer) that the project has selected. That happens when the person chooses Printer settings… in the header on a project that uses a stock profile. In that case, changes to the nozzle and to the connection are refused with `stock_profile`. Changes to settings are saved as a copy of the profile, and the conversation follows that copy from then on (`PrinterConversation::tool_settled`). A Change conversation is never turned into an Add conversation. The code that opens a Change conversation checks that the printer is there, and shows OrcaSlicer's error dialog when it is not.
186-
187-The header's filament chat uses the same panel (`PrinterPanel::open_filament`). It is offered the four settings tools and nothing else, and it gets no project state. It has its own instructions. The page writes them in `AgentUI/src/filamentInstructions.ts` and sends them with `filament_instructions`. The page writes them from the facts the app sends as the session part of the panel's state (`PrinterPanel::filament_session_json`): the preset's name, its slot and material, and, for a stock filament, the copy that a change is saved as. The preflight check for this chat allows the settings tools only with `scope: "filament"` on that preset. It refuses an apply that has no `persistAs`, with `not_saved`, because the chat is gone when it closes. When a copy is saved in the preset's place, the chat is about that copy from then on, and the page writes the instructions again for the copy. Until 2026-09-29 the filament chat ran on the project assistant's instructions and tools. With those, the model read "make the nozzle 5 degrees hotter" as a request to print. In another run it set 205 °C when the value was 220 °C, without reading the value first.
188-
--
277-The registry cannot change while the app runs, and its entries always come in the same order. A tool adapter may leave tools out, based on the exposure each tool declares. An adapter must not change a tool's action class, validation, or behavior. Keep the list that MCP clients see stable. The only exception would be a server that also implements and tests the current protocol's notification for a changed tool list. When a tool cannot run because of the app's current state, report that from `tools/call` instead of removing the tool from the list.
278-
279:`ToolDefinition` currently stores the name, title, description, input and output schemas, action class, exposure, availability, and handler. The other properties are not registry fields. Whether a tool is revision-sensitive, whether it is all-or-nothing, how it cancels, and how it appears in history are all determined by the coordinator and workspace code, and checked by their tests. `ToolAvailability` currently describes the session a tool is offered in (`Always`, or `SkillIndex` for `skill_read` when the page lists skills). It does not filter tools by the current state of the project or by what one message carries: on Anthropic the tools open every request, so a list that changes between requests of a chat voids that chat's whole prompt cache. `object_import` is offered on every turn, and a call that names no attached model file fails with `invalid_arguments`.
280-
281-Inputs are validated by the `valid_arguments` decoder that the registry has for each handler. Changing only the JSON Schema does not change which calls are accepted. Successful MCP output is checked by `validate_output`, which deliberately understands only a small set of schema keywords. Before you use a keyword it does not support, extend the validator and add tests. Do not assume that `validate_output` implements all of JSON Schema, or that every adapter validates output automatically.

# Web search instead of the connection skill, 2026-11-02

I gave the printer chat Anthropic's `web_search` tool and left out the `connect-bambu` skill. Four live chats on the real P1S, with `claude-sonnet-5-5`, cost $0.11 in total. **The agent never searched once.** Every fact it gave came from its own knowledge, so these chats do not show whether search can supply what the skill knows.

## What I changed
The code is on branch `claude/connect-web-search`, uncommitted. All of it is test-only, behind environment variables:
- `JUSPRIN_TEST_WEB_SEARCH` adds the basic search tool (`web_search_20250305`, at most 5 searches a request) and keeps the skill out of the chat.
- The codec keeps search queries and citations when it sends a reply back.
- `JUSPRIN_TEST_HEAR_NOTHING` makes the app ignore the printers it hears, and a new `no-printer` scenario uses it.

The prompt, the tools and the app's notes are unchanged.

## The chats
Kenneth had restarted the printer, and it answered port 8883 in 10 to 123 ms. The skill's earlier chats ran while it was slow and got code -1, so they are not a like-for-like comparison.

| Chat | Requests | Searches | Wall time | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Normal connect | 4 | 0 | 42 s | $0.029 |
| Wrong code, twice | 8 | 0 | 65 s | $0.042 |
| Right code | 7 | 0 | 45 s | $0.012 |
| No printer heard | 7 | 0 | 150 s | $0.024 |

**Wrong code.** The app said "The printer refused the access code." The agent said: "My guess is a small typo, or the code on the printer has changed. Some printers show a new code after LAN mode is switched off and on." After the second refusal: "The code was refused a second time, so I don't think a typo is the cause. My new guess is that the printer I found isn't yours." It asked whether the screen shows 192.168.0.198. These are reasonable, labelled guesses with a cheap check.

**Right code.** It connected, and the agent said the person can close the chat.

**No printer heard.** First guess: off, other Wi-Fi, guest network or VPN. Told those were ruled out: "My next guess is that the printer isn't in LAN mode." **That is wrong:** a printer with LAN Only off is still heard, and the app reports it as in cloud mode. The skill says so, and the agent had no way to know. Told LAN Only is on, it moved to the firewall, AP isolation, or a mesh or extender. It never only waited, so the regression the skill caused (`connect-bambu-not-found`) did not appear.

## Problems
1. **No search ever ran.** The tool was offered: the cached prompt grew by the tool's 2,500 tokens. The model chose its own knowledge each time.
2. **A menu location stated as fact.** It told the person twice that the code is on the printer's screen "in its network settings" without calling it a guess. In the first chat it called the same claim a guess. I have not checked whether this is right for a P1S.
3. **The harness check misfires.** `live_p1s_words_do_not_say_no_printer` failed in three chats on the choice "I can't find it", which is about the code.

## Not tested
- A chat in which a search actually ran, so where the results come from and whether they are right for this printer.
- The 18 scripted suite cases, and a no-printer chat with the skill as a control.
- Failures on a slow printer, search with dynamic filtering, and showing sources to the person.

## Recommendation
Keep the skill. Search alone added nothing, because the model did not use it. The one fact the agent got wrong, LAN Only off is still heard, is how this app works, and a search would not find it. Search might still help with menus on printers the team has never tested. That needs a prompt line telling the model to look them up before guessing, which is Kenneth's call to approve and test.

174-**The printer panel follows the same rule with its own set of tools.** The printer panel on Home runs its own conversation, `PrinterConversation`. That conversation is offered the five printer tools and the four settings tools. The list is the same in every mode (Add, Change, or Connect), so it stays byte-identical through a conversation and between conversations of the same mode.
175-
176:One tool is added during a conversation, on purpose. `issue_report_open` comes with the Bambu connection skill (`PrinterConversation::connection_skill`, carried as `AgentSkillUse::tools`). It is offered from the request where the skill is first sent, including the continuation after the tool result that brought the skill, and on every request after that. A chat where the person never tries to connect never has it. Adding it costs that chat one prompt-cache miss, and that cost was accepted. The list stays the same from then on. This is not deferral: no tool search, no `defer_loading`, and no toolsets. The app decides when the tool is offered, and the model never asks for it.
177-
178-What a call may do depends on the conversation. `PrinterConversation::preflight_tool` refuses every call that is not allowed, before any card is shown, with an error that says where to go instead. The rules are:
179-
180-- Finding and adding a printer (`printer_identify`, `printer_add`) is allowed only in an Add conversation. A Change or Connect conversation is about a printer the person already has. An add there would save another printer and move the conversation onto it.
181-- `printer_change` is allowed only on the printer the conversation is about, once there is one. When the project uses that printer, its unsaved edits are dropped and listed in `discarded`; the panel's coordinator saves a version first, as the project's agent pane does for any change to the project. If that save fails, the call does not run and returns the coordinator's generic `local_save_failed`; there is no separate message for it.
182-- The connection tools are allowed only once there is a saved printer.
183-- The settings tools are allowed only with `scope: "printer"`, on the printer the conversation is about.
184-
185-A Change conversation may be about a stock profile (one that ships with OrcaSlicer) that the project has selected. That happens when the person chooses Printer settings… in the header on a project that uses a stock profile. In that case, changes to the nozzle and to the connection are refused with `stock_profile`. Changes to settings are saved as a copy of the profile, and the conversation follows that copy from then on (`PrinterConversation::tool_settled`). A Change conversation is never turned into an Add conversation. The code that opens a Change conversation checks that the printer is there, and shows OrcaSlicer's error dialog when it is not.
186-
187-The header's filament chat uses the same panel (`PrinterPanel::open_filament`). It is offered the four settings tools and nothing else, and it gets no project state. It has its own instructions. The page writes them in `AgentUI/src/filamentInstructions.ts` and sends them with `filament_instructions`. The page writes them from the facts the app sends as the session part of the panel's state (`PrinterPanel::filament_session_json`): the preset's name, its slot and material, and, for a stock filament, the copy that a change is saved as. The preflight check for this chat allows the settings tools only with `scope: "filament"` on that preset. It refuses an apply that has no `persistAs`, with `not_saved`, because the chat is gone when it closes. When a copy is saved in the preset's place, the chat is about that copy from then on, and the page writes the instructions again for the copy. Until 2026-09-29 the filament chat ran on the project assistant's instructions and tools. With those, the model read "make the nozzle 5 degrees hotter" as a request to print. In another run it set 205 °C when the value was 220 °C, without reading the value first.
188-
--
277-The registry cannot change while the app runs, and its entries always come in the same order. A tool adapter may leave tools out, based on the exposure each tool declares. An adapter must not change a tool's action class, validation, or behavior. Keep the list that MCP clients see stable. The only exception would be a server that also implements and tests the current protocol's notification for a changed tool list. When a tool cannot run because of the app's current state, report that from `tools/call` instead of removing the tool from the list.
278-
279:`ToolDefinition` currently stores the name, title, description, input and output schemas, action class, exposure, availability, and handler. The other properties are not registry fields. Whether a tool is revision-sensitive, whether it is all-or-nothing, how it cancels, and how it appears in history are all determined by the coordinator and workspace code, and checked by their tests. `ToolAvailability` currently describes the session a tool is offered in (`Always`, or `SkillIndex` for `skill_read` when the page lists skills). It does not filter tools by the current state of the project or by what one message carries: on Anthropic the tools open every request, so a list that changes between requests of a chat voids that chat's whole prompt cache. `object_import` is offered on every turn, and a call that names no attached model file fails with `invalid_arguments`.
280-
281-Inputs are validated by the `valid_arguments` decoder that the registry has for each handler. Changing only the JSON Schema does not change which calls are accepted. Successful MCP output is checked by `validate_output`, which deliberately understands only a small set of schema keywords. Before you use a keyword it does not support, extend the validator and add tests. Do not assume that `validate_output` implements all of JSON Schema, or that every adapter validates output automatically.

# CLAUDE.md - Testing Guide for OrcaSlicer

This guide provides comprehensive instructions for Claude Code when writing, maintaining, and understanding tests in the OrcaSlicer codebase.

## ⚠️ CRITICAL RULES - MUST FOLLOW

### 1. **SECTIONS IN LOOPS - NEVER REUSE NAMES**
❌ **WRONG**: Will cause unpredictable behavior
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Bad loop sections") {
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
        SECTION("Same name") {  // WRONG! Same name used multiple times
            REQUIRE(i >= 0);
        }
    }
}
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Use DYNAMIC_SECTION or incorporate counter
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Good loop sections") {
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
        DYNAMIC_SECTION("Section " << i) {  // Unique name per iteration
            REQUIRE(i >= 0);
        }
    }
}
```

### 2. **THREAD SAFETY - ASSERTIONS ARE NOT THREAD-SAFE**
❌ **WRONG**: Will cause undefined behavior or crashes
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Multi-threaded test") {
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
        threads.emplace_back([]() {
            REQUIRE(some_calculation() == expected);  // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
        });
    }
}
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Synchronize results, test on main thread
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Multi-threaded test") {
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    std::atomic<int> passed{0};
    
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
        threads.emplace_back([&passed]() {
            if (some_calculation() == expected) {
                passed++;
            }
        });
    }
    
    for (auto& t : threads) t.join();
    REQUIRE(passed == 4);  // Test results on main thread
}
```

### 3. **EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION - AVOID BINARY OPERATORS**
❌ **WRONG**: Cannot decompose properly
```cpp
REQUIRE(a > 0 && b < 10);  // Shows "false" on failure, not individual values
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Split into separate assertions
```cpp
REQUIRE(a > 0);
REQUIRE(b < 10);  // Each shows individual values on failure
```

### 4. **FLOATING POINT - NEVER USE APPROX**
❌ **WRONG**: Approx is deprecated and asymmetric
```cpp
REQUIRE(calculated_value == Catch::Approx(expected));  // Deprecated!
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Use floating point matchers
```cpp
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinAbs(expected, 0.001));
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinRel(expected, 0.01));  // 1% tolerance
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinULP(expected, 4));     // 4 ULPs apart
```

### 5. **TEST ORDERING - ALWAYS USE RANDOM ORDER**
✅ **REQUIRED**: For CI/CD and development
```bash
# Essential flags for running tests
./tests --order rand --warn NoAssertions

# For test sharding (parallel execution), share random seed
./tests --order rand --shard-index 0 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
./tests --order rand --shard-index 1 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
./tests --order rand --shard-index 2 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
```

## Overview of OrcaSlicer's Testing Framework

OrcaSlicer uses **Catch2 v3** (currently v3.11.0, vendored in `tests/catch2/`) as its primary testing framework. The test suite is organized into several modules that mirror the project's architectural components:

> **Note**: Test files include the framework via `#include <catch2/catch_all.hpp>` (the v3 single-header convenience include). All v3 features described in this guide are available.

### Test Structure
```
tests/
├── CMakeLists.txt              # Main test configuration
├── catch_main.hpp              # Custom test reporter
├── libslic3r/                  # Core library tests (21 test files)
├── fff_print/                  # FFF printing tests (12 test files)
├── sla_print/                  # SLA printing tests (4 test files)
├── libnest2d/                  # 2D nesting tests
├── slic3rutils/               # Utility tests
├── data/                      # Test data files and meshes
└── catch2/                    # Catch2 framework files
```

### Build Integration
- Tests are built using CMake with `catch_discover_tests()` integration
- Each test module creates a separate executable (e.g., `libslic3r_tests`, `fff_print_tests`)
- Test data directory is available via `TEST_DATA_DIR` preprocessor definition
- Custom verbose console reporter provides detailed test output

## Test Suite Organization

### libslic3r Tests
Core slicing engine tests covering:
- **Geometry operations**: Points, polygons, lines, Voronoi diagrams
- **File formats**: STL, 3MF, AMF parsing and validation
- **Algorithms**: Clipper operations, mesh boolean operations, optimization
- **Configuration**: Print settings validation and parsing
- **Utilities**: String processing, time utilities, data structures

### fff_print Tests
Fused Filament Fabrication specific tests:
- **G-code generation**: Writer functionality, cooling, lift/unlift
- **Slicing algorithms**: Layer generation, infill patterns
- **Print mechanics**: Flow calculations, extrusion, support material
- **Model processing**: Print objects, skirt/brim generation

### sla_print Tests
Stereolithography specific tests:
- **SLA print processing**: Layer curing, support generation
- **Raycast operations**: Light path calculations
- **Test utilities**: SLA-specific helper functions

## Writing New Tests - Best Practices

### File Organization
1. **Naming Convention**: `test_<feature>.cpp` (e.g., `test_geometry.cpp`)
2. **Header Structure**: Include `<catch2/catch_all.hpp>` first, then relevant headers
3. **Namespace Usage**: Use `using namespace Slic3r;` for convenience
4. **File Placement**: Add to appropriate test directory and update CMakeLists.txt

### Test Naming and Structure
```cpp
#include <catch2/catch_all.hpp>
#include "libslic3r/Point.hpp"

using namespace Slic3r;

TEST_CASE("Feature description", "[category_tag]") {
    // Test implementation
}
```

### Tagging System
Use descriptive tags for test categorization:
- `[Geometry]` - Geometric operations and calculations
- `[GCodeWriter]` - G-code generation functionality  
- `[Config]` - Configuration and settings tests
- `[FileFormat]` - File I/O operations (STL, 3MF, etc.)
- `[Algorithm]` - Core algorithms and processing
- `[Performance]` - Performance benchmarks (if applicable)

## Catch2 Features Guide

### Basic Assertions
```cpp
// Primary assertions - stop test on failure
REQUIRE(expression);
REQUIRE_FALSE(expression);

// Continuing assertions - continue test after failure  
CHECK(expression);
CHECK_FALSE(expression);

// Non-failing checks - record result but don't fail test
CHECK_NOFAIL(expression);  // Useful for assumptions that might be violated
```

### Exception Testing
```cpp
// Verify no exception is thrown
REQUIRE_NOTHROW(function_call());

// Verify any exception is thrown
REQUIRE_THROWS(risky_function());

// Verify specific exception type
REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(function_call(), SpecificException);

// Verify exception message
REQUIRE_THROWS_WITH(function_call(), "Expected error message");

// Verify exception with matchers (for partial matching)
REQUIRE_THROWS_MATCHES(function_call(), SpecificException, 
                       Catch::Matchers::Message("contains this"));
```

### Complex Assertions with Matchers
```cpp
#include <catch2/matchers/catch_matchers.hpp>

// String matchers
using Catch::Matchers::StartsWith;
using Catch::Matchers::EndsWith;
using Catch::Matchers::ContainsSubstring;
using Catch::Matchers::Equals;
using Catch::Matchers::Matches;  // Regex matching

REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, StartsWith("Expected prefix"));
REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, ContainsSubstring("middle part"));
REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, Matches(".*pattern.*"));

// Floating point matchers - ALWAYS use these instead of Approx!
using Catch::Matchers::WithinAbs;
using Catch::Matchers::WithinRel;
using Catch::Matchers::WithinULP;

REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinAbs(expected, 0.001));     // Absolute tolerance
REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinRel(expected, 0.01));      // Relative tolerance (1%)
REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinULP(expected, 4));         // ULP difference (requires IEEE-754)

// Combining matchers
REQUIRE_THAT(value, WithinRel(expected, 0.001) || WithinAbs(0.0, 0.000001));
```

### Sections for Test Organization
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Complex feature testing", "[Feature]") {
    // Common setup code
    SomeObject obj;
    
    SECTION("First scenario") {
        // Specific test case
        REQUIRE(obj.method1() == expected_value);
    }
    
    SECTION("Second scenario") {
        // Another test case with same setup
        REQUIRE(obj.method2() == other_expected);
    }
}
```

### BDD-Style Tests
Use for complex scenarios and user story testing:

> **Note**: BDD macros are aliases for TEST_CASE and SECTION with prefixed names
```cpp
SCENARIO("User performs complex operation", "[UserStory]") {
    GIVEN("A specific setup condition") {
        GCodeWriter writer;
        // Setup code
        
        WHEN("User performs action") {
            auto result = writer.some_operation();
            
            THEN("Expected outcome occurs") {
                REQUIRE(result.size() > 0);
                
                AND_WHEN("Follow-up action occurs") {
                    auto next_result = writer.next_operation();
                    
                    THEN("Final outcome is correct") {
                        REQUIRE(next_result == expected);
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

### Data Generators for Parameterized Tests
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Function works with various inputs", "[Algorithm]") {
    auto test_value = GENERATE(1, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13);
    
    REQUIRE(is_odd(test_value));
    REQUIRE(test_value > 0);
}

// Range-based generators
TEST_CASE("Range testing", "[Algorithm]") {
    auto i = GENERATE(range(1, 10));  // 1 to 9
    REQUIRE(process_value(i) > i);
}

// Using variables in generators (requires GENERATE_COPY or GENERATE_REF)
TEST_CASE("Generator with variables", "[Algorithm]") {
    std::vector<int> values = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
    auto test_value = GENERATE_REF(from_range(values));  // Use GENERATE_REF for references
    
    REQUIRE(test_value > 0);
}

// Custom generators
TEST_CASE("Random values", "[Algorithm]") {
    auto random_int = GENERATE(take(100, random(-1000, 1000)));  // 100 random values
    REQUIRE(process_random_value(random_int));
}
```

### Test Fixtures
```cpp
class GeometryFixture {
public:
    Point origin{0, 0};
    Point unit_x{1, 0};
    Point unit_y{0, 1};
    
    mutable double tolerance = EPSILON;  // Use mutable for data that might change
};

// Standard fixture - new instance per test run
TEST_CASE_METHOD(GeometryFixture, "Point operations", "[Geometry]") {
    REQUIRE(origin.distance_to(unit_x) == 1.0);
}

// Persistent fixture - single instance for entire test case (v3.2.0+)
TEST_CASE_PERSISTENT_FIXTURE(GeometryFixture, "Persistent operations", "[Geometry]") {
    static int call_count = 0;
    ++call_count;
    INFO("This fixture persists across sections, call: " << call_count);
    
    SECTION("First section") {
        REQUIRE(origin.distance_to(unit_x) == 1.0);
    }
    
    SECTION("Second section") {
        REQUIRE(origin.distance_to(unit_y) == 1.0);
        // call_count will be 2 here with persistent fixture
    }
}

// Template fixtures for type-parameterized tests
template<typename T>
class NumericFixture {
public:
    T zero = T{0};
    T one = T{1};
};

TEMPLATE_TEST_CASE_METHOD(NumericFixture, "Numeric operations", "[Template]", int, float, double) {
    REQUIRE(TestType{} == this->zero);
    REQUIRE(TestType{1} == this->one);
}
```

### Advanced Testing Features

#### Logging and Information Macros
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Advanced logging", "[Logging]") {
    INFO("This info persists until end of scope");
    
    SECTION("Section A") {
        INFO("Section A specific info");
        CAPTURE(some_variable, another_var);  // Captures variable names and values
        CHECK(some_condition);
    }
    
    SECTION("Section B") {
        UNSCOPED_INFO("This survives beyond its scope");  // v2.7.0+
        CHECK(other_condition);
    }
}

// Warning and explicit control
TEST_CASE("Explicit test control", "[Control]") {
    WARN("This warns but doesn't fail the test");
    
    if (precondition_not_met) {
        SKIP("Reason");  // Marks the test as skipped (v3.3.0+, available)
        return;
    }
    
    if (critical_failure) {
        FAIL("Critical condition failed");  // Fails and stops test
    }
    
    SUCCEED("Reached successful completion");  // Explicit success marker
}
```

#### Static Assertions (Compile-time Testing)
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Compile-time checks", "[Static]") {
    STATIC_REQUIRE(sizeof(int) >= 4);  // Checked at compile time
    STATIC_REQUIRE_FALSE(std::is_void_v<int>);
    
    // For traits and template metaprogramming
    STATIC_CHECK(std::is_trivially_copyable_v<Point>);  // v3.0.1+
}
```

#### Conditional Testing
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Conditional blocks", "[Conditional]") {
    int value = get_test_value();
    
    // These record the expression but don't count as test failures (v3.0.1+)
    CHECKED_IF(value > 0) {
        // This block runs if value > 0
        REQUIRE(value <= 100);
    } CHECKED_ELSE(value > 0) {
        // This block runs if value <= 0  
        REQUIRE(value >= -100);
    }
}
```

#### Benchmarking (v2.9.0+)
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Performance testing", "[Benchmark]") {
    // Simple benchmarking
    BENCHMARK("Algorithm performance") {
        return expensive_algorithm();
    };
    
    // Advanced benchmarking with setup
    BENCHMARK_ADVANCED("Advanced benchmark")(Catch::Benchmark::Chronometer meter) {
        std::vector<int> data = setup_test_data();  // Setup not measured
        
        meter.measure([&] { 
            return process_data(data);  // Only this is measured
        });
    };
}
```

## OrcaSlicer-Specific Testing Patterns

### Geometry Testing
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Line operations", "[Geometry]") {
    Line line{{100000, 0}, {0, 0}};
    Line parallel{{200000, 0}, {0, 0}};
    
    REQUIRE(line.parallel_to(line));
    REQUIRE(line.parallel_to(parallel));
    
    // Test with epsilon tolerance
    Line rotated(parallel);

## Running and Debugging Tests

### Building Tests
```bash
# Build all tests
cd build && make

# Build specific test suite
cd build && make libslic3r_tests

# Build and run tests
cd build && make && ctest

### Running Tests

#### Essential Test Execution Patterns
```bash
# REQUIRED: Random order with assertion warnings (best practice)
cd build && ./tests/libslic3r/libslic3r_tests --order rand --warn NoAssertions

# Run all tests with verbose output via CTest
cd build && ctest --output-on-failure

# Run specific test suite with best practices
cd build && ./tests/libslic3r/libslic3r_tests --order rand --warn NoAssertions

# Filter tests with specific tags
cd build && ./tests/libslic3r/libslic3r_tests "[Geometry]" --order rand

# Filter by test name patterns
cd build && ./tests/libslic3r/libslic3r_tests "*geometry*" --order rand

# Exclude tests (negation)

# Combine filters: (Geometry AND Config) OR Algorithm

# List available tests, tags, and reporters
cd build && ./tests/libslic3r/libslic3r_tests --list-tests
cd build && ./tests/libslic3r/libslic3r_tests --list-tags  
cd build && ./tests/libslic3r/libslic3r_tests --list-reporters

# Debug failing tests

cd build && ./tests/libslic3r/libslic3r_tests --success  # Show passing tests too
cd build && ./tests/libslic3r/libslic3r_tests --durations yes  # Show timing info

cd build && ./tests/libslic3r/libslic3r_tests --order rand --shard-index 1 --shard-count 4 --rng-seed 0xBEEF &
cd build && ./tests/libslic3r/libslic3r_tests --order rand --shard-index 2 --shard-count 4 --rng-seed 0xBEEF &

wait  # Wait for all to complete
```

## Test Data Management

### Using TEST_DATA_DIR
All test data is accessible via the `TEST_DATA_DIR` preprocessor definition:

```cpp
std::string mesh_path = std::string(TEST_DATA_DIR) + "/20mm_cube.obj";
std::string config_path = std::string(TEST_DATA_DIR) + "/test_config/printer.ini";
```

### Available Test Assets

#### 3D Models
- **Basic shapes**: `20mm_cube.obj`, `pyramid.obj`, `sphere.obj`
- **Complex geometry**: `extruder_idler.obj`, `ipadstand.obj`, `bridge.obj`
- **Edge cases**: `cube_with_hole.obj`, `sloping_hole.obj`, `small_dorito.obj`

#### File Format Tests

#### Test Utilities
The `Test` namespace provides helper functions:

using namespace Slic3r::Test;

// Load standard test meshes
TriangleMesh mesh = mesh(TestMesh::cube_20x20x20);

// Standard test configurations

```

## Common Pitfalls and Solutions

### Floating-Point Comparisons

> **CRITICAL**: Never use Approx - it's deprecated due to asymmetry and other issues

❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
REQUIRE(calculated_volume == expected_volume);           // Exact equality
REQUIRE(calculated_volume == Catch::Approx(expected));   // Deprecated! Asymmetric!
```

✅ **Correct**: Always use floating point matchers
```cpp
// Absolute tolerance - good when values are near zero
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinAbs(expected_volume, 0.001));

// Relative tolerance - good for values with different magnitudes
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinRel(expected_volume, 0.01));  // 1% tolerance

// ULP (Units in Last Place) - most precise, requires IEEE-754
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinULP(expected_volume, 4));

// Combined approach - relative OR absolute
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, 
    WithinRel(expected_volume, 0.001) || WithinAbs(0.0, 0.000001));

// Precision control for output
Catch::StringMaker<double>::precision = 15;  // Show more decimal places
```

### Why Approx is Problematic:
- **Asymmetric**: `Approx(10).epsilon(0.1) != 11.1` but `Approx(11.1).epsilon(0.1) == 10`
- **Double-only**: All computation done in `double`, causes issues with `float` inputs  
- **Default behavior**: Only uses relative comparison, so `Approx(0) == X` only works for `X == 0`

### Path Handling
❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
std::string path = TEST_DATA_DIR + "/model.obj";  // May have path separator issues
```

✅ **Correct**:
```cpp
std::string path = std::string(TEST_DATA_DIR) + "/model.obj";
// or use boost::filesystem for complex path operations
```

### Exception Testing
❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
bool threw_exception = false;
try {
    risky_function();
} catch (...) {
    threw_exception = true;
}
REQUIRE(threw_exception);
```

✅ **Correct**:
```cpp
REQUIRE_THROWS(risky_function());
// or for specific exceptions
REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(risky_function(), SpecificException);
```

### Thread Safety

⚠️ **CRITICAL**: Catch2 assertions are **NOT thread-safe** by default!

> **Note**: Catch2 v3.9.0+ has opt-in thread-safe assertions via `CATCH_CONFIG_EXPERIMENTAL_THREAD_SAFE_ASSERTIONS`. OrcaSlicer is on v3.11.0 but does not enable this flag, so assertions remain non-thread-safe by default.

❌ **Incorrect**: Will cause undefined behavior or crashes
```cpp
std::thread t([&]() {
    REQUIRE(threaded_operation() == expected);  // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
    CHECK(other_operation());                   // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
});
```

✅ **Correct**: Collect results, assert on main thread
```cpp
std::atomic<bool> success{false};
std::atomic<int> error_count{0};

std::thread t([&]() {
    // Do work in thread, collect results
    bool result1 = (threaded_operation() == expected);
    bool result2 = other_operation();
    
    if (result1 && result2) {
        success = true;
    } else {
        error_count++;
    }
});

t.join();

// Assert results on main thread
REQUIRE(success);
REQUIRE(error_count == 0);
```

#### Thread Safety Rules:
- **REQUIRE family**: Would terminate process in spawned threads (throws exception with no try-catch)
- **CHECK family**: Not thread-safe, can corrupt internal state
- **SKIP, FAIL, SUCCEED**: Not thread-safe even with v3 thread-safe assertions
- **Message macros**: INFO, CAPTURE, WARN - not thread-safe
- **STATIC_REQUIRE/CHECK**: Not thread-safe (relies on runtime registration)

### Memory Management
Use RAII and smart pointers in tests:
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Resource management", "[Memory]") {
    auto model = std::make_unique<Model>();
    // Automatic cleanup on test completion/failure
    
    REQUIRE(model->objects.empty());
}
```

## Integration with CMake

### Adding New Test Files
1. Create test file: `test_new_feature.cpp`
2. Add to appropriate `CMakeLists.txt`:
```cmake

### Advanced Test Discovery

)

```

### Conditional Test Compilation
```cmake
# Feature-dependent tests

    target_sources(${_TEST_NAME}_tests PRIVATE test_hollowing.cpp)
endif()

# Platform-specific tests
if(WIN32)
    target_sources(${_TEST_NAME}_tests PRIVATE test_windows_specific.cpp)

endif()
```

## Known Issues and Workarounds

### Platform-Specific Issues
```cpp
// MinGW/CygWin slow linking workaround
// Use: -fuse-ld=lld flag to speed up linking significantly

// Visual Studio 2017 raw string literal bug
#define CATCH_CONFIG_DISABLE_STRINGIFICATION
// This disables expression stringification but works around the compiler bug

// Visual Studio 2022 spaceship operator issue
// REQUIRE((a <=> b) == 0);  // May not compile with MSVC
// Workaround: use clang-cl or avoid spaceship in assertions

// QNX/VxWorks C stdlib issues

std::foo_function();     // Always call qualified
// NOT: #include <foo.h> and foo_function();
```

### Catch2 v3 Features Available
```cpp
// OrcaSlicer is on Catch2 v3.11.0 - all of these ARE available:
// SKIP() macro                           - v3.3.0+
// Opt-in thread-safe assertions          - v3.9.0+ (NOT enabled here; see Thread Safety)
// Built-in BENCHMARK / BENCHMARK_ADVANCED - v3.x

// STATIC_CHECK macro                     - v3.0.1+
// Built-in test sharding (--shard-*)     - v3.x

// v3 notes to remember:
// - String matcher is "ContainsSubstring" (v2's "Contains" no longer exists)
// - Sections can still be re-run if a later section fails (unchanged from v2)
```

### Test Organization Best Practices

#### Project Structure Rules
1. **1:1 correspondence**: One test binary per library/module
2. **Hidden tests**: Use `[.]` or `[!benchmark]` tags for tests that shouldn't run by default
3. **Tag hierarchy**: Use consistent tagging scheme across the project
4. **File naming**: Follow `test_<feature>.cpp` pattern

#### CI/CD Integration
```bash

./tests --order rand --warn NoAssertions --reporter junit::out=results.xml

# For coverage analysis
./tests --order rand --warn NoAssertions --reporter console --success

# For performance tracking

```

# CLAUDE.md - Testing Guide for OrcaSlicer

This guide provides comprehensive instructions for Claude Code when writing, maintaining, and understanding tests in the OrcaSlicer codebase.

## ⚠️ CRITICAL RULES - MUST FOLLOW

### 1. **SECTIONS IN LOOPS - NEVER REUSE NAMES**
❌ **WRONG**: Will cause unpredictable behavior
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Bad loop sections") {
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
        SECTION("Same name") {  // WRONG! Same name used multiple times
            REQUIRE(i >= 0);
        }
    }
}
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Use DYNAMIC_SECTION or incorporate counter
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Good loop sections") {
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
        DYNAMIC_SECTION("Section " << i) {  // Unique name per iteration
            REQUIRE(i >= 0);
        }
    }
}
```

### 2. **THREAD SAFETY - ASSERTIONS ARE NOT THREAD-SAFE**
❌ **WRONG**: Will cause undefined behavior or crashes
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Multi-threaded test") {
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
        threads.emplace_back([]() {
            REQUIRE(some_calculation() == expected);  // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
        });
    }
}
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Synchronize results, test on main thread
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Multi-threaded test") {
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    std::atomic<int> passed{0};
    
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
        threads.emplace_back([&passed]() {
            if (some_calculation() == expected) {
                passed++;
            }
        });
    }
    
    for (auto& t : threads) t.join();
    REQUIRE(passed == 4);  // Test results on main thread
}
```

### 3. **EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION - AVOID BINARY OPERATORS**
❌ **WRONG**: Cannot decompose properly
```cpp
REQUIRE(a > 0 && b < 10);  // Shows "false" on failure, not individual values
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Split into separate assertions
```cpp
REQUIRE(a > 0);
REQUIRE(b < 10);  // Each shows individual values on failure
```

### 4. **FLOATING POINT - NEVER USE APPROX**
❌ **WRONG**: Approx is deprecated and asymmetric
```cpp
REQUIRE(calculated_value == Catch::Approx(expected));  // Deprecated!
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Use floating point matchers
```cpp
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinAbs(expected, 0.001));
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinRel(expected, 0.01));  // 1% tolerance
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinULP(expected, 4));     // 4 ULPs apart
```

### 5. **TEST ORDERING - ALWAYS USE RANDOM ORDER**
✅ **REQUIRED**: For CI/CD and development
```bash
# Essential flags for running tests
./tests --order rand --warn NoAssertions

# For test sharding (parallel execution), share random seed
./tests --order rand --shard-index 0 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
./tests --order rand --shard-index 1 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
./tests --order rand --shard-index 2 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
```

## Overview of OrcaSlicer's Testing Framework

OrcaSlicer uses **Catch2 v3** (currently v3.11.0, vendored in `tests/catch2/`) as its primary testing framework. The test suite is organized into several modules that mirror the project's architectural components:

> **Note**: Test files include the framework via `#include <catch2/catch_all.hpp>` (the v3 single-header convenience include). All v3 features described in this guide are available.

### Test Structure
```
tests/
├── CMakeLists.txt              # Main test configuration
├── catch_main.hpp              # Custom test reporter
├── libslic3r/                  # Core library tests (21 test files)
├── fff_print/                  # FFF printing tests (12 test files)
├── sla_print/                  # SLA printing tests (4 test files)
├── libnest2d/                  # 2D nesting tests
├── slic3rutils/               # Utility tests
├── data/                      # Test data files and meshes
└── catch2/                    # Catch2 framework files
```

### Build Integration
- Tests are built using CMake with `catch_discover_tests()` integration
- Each test module creates a separate executable (e.g., `libslic3r_tests`, `fff_print_tests`)
- Test data directory is available via `TEST_DATA_DIR` preprocessor definition
- Custom verbose console reporter provides detailed test output

## Test Suite Organization

### libslic3r Tests
Core slicing engine tests covering:
- **Geometry operations**: Points, polygons, lines, Voronoi diagrams
- **File formats**: STL, 3MF, AMF parsing and validation
- **Algorithms**: Clipper operations, mesh boolean operations, optimization
- **Configuration**: Print settings validation and parsing
- **Utilities**: String processing, time utilities, data structures

### fff_print Tests
Fused Filament Fabrication specific tests:
- **G-code generation**: Writer functionality, cooling, lift/unlift
- **Slicing algorithms**: Layer generation, infill patterns
- **Print mechanics**: Flow calculations, extrusion, support material
- **Model processing**: Print objects, skirt/brim generation

### sla_print Tests
Stereolithography specific tests:
- **SLA print processing**: Layer curing, support generation
- **Raycast operations**: Light path calculations
- **Test utilities**: SLA-specific helper functions

## Writing New Tests - Best Practices

### File Organization
1. **Naming Convention**: `test_<feature>.cpp` (e.g., `test_geometry.cpp`)
2. **Header Structure**: Include `<catch2/catch_all.hpp>` first, then relevant headers
3. **Namespace Usage**: Use `using namespace Slic3r;` for convenience
4. **File Placement**: Add to appropriate test directory and update CMakeLists.txt

### Test Naming and Structure
```cpp
#include <catch2/catch_all.hpp>
#include "libslic3r/Point.hpp"

using namespace Slic3r;

TEST_CASE("Feature description", "[category_tag]") {
    // Test implementation
}
```

### Tagging System
Use descriptive tags for test categorization:
- `[Geometry]` - Geometric operations and calculations
- `[GCodeWriter]` - G-code generation functionality  
- `[Config]` - Configuration and settings tests
- `[FileFormat]` - File I/O operations (STL, 3MF, etc.)
- `[Algorithm]` - Core algorithms and processing
- `[Performance]` - Performance benchmarks (if applicable)

## Catch2 Features Guide

### Basic Assertions
```cpp
// Primary assertions - stop test on failure
REQUIRE(expression);
REQUIRE_FALSE(expression);

// Continuing assertions - continue test after failure  
CHECK(expression);
CHECK_FALSE(expression);

// Non-failing checks - record result but don't fail test
CHECK_NOFAIL(expression);  // Useful for assumptions that might be violated
```

### Exception Testing
```cpp
// Verify no exception is thrown
REQUIRE_NOTHROW(function_call());

// Verify any exception is thrown
REQUIRE_THROWS(risky_function());

// Verify specific exception type
REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(function_call(), SpecificException);

// Verify exception message
REQUIRE_THROWS_WITH(function_call(), "Expected error message");

// Verify exception with matchers (for partial matching)
REQUIRE_THROWS_MATCHES(function_call(), SpecificException, 
                       Catch::Matchers::Message("contains this"));
```

### Complex Assertions with Matchers
```cpp
#include <catch2/matchers/catch_matchers.hpp>

// String matchers
using Catch::Matchers::StartsWith;
using Catch::Matchers::EndsWith;
using Catch::Matchers::ContainsSubstring;
using Catch::Matchers::Equals;
using Catch::Matchers::Matches;  // Regex matching

REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, StartsWith("Expected prefix"));
REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, ContainsSubstring("middle part"));
REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, Matches(".*pattern.*"));

// Floating point matchers - ALWAYS use these instead of Approx!
using Catch::Matchers::WithinAbs;
using Catch::Matchers::WithinRel;
using Catch::Matchers::WithinULP;

REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinAbs(expected, 0.001));     // Absolute tolerance
REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinRel(expected, 0.01));      // Relative tolerance (1%)
REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinULP(expected, 4));         // ULP difference (requires IEEE-754)

// Combining matchers
REQUIRE_THAT(value, WithinRel(expected, 0.001) || WithinAbs(0.0, 0.000001));
```

### Sections for Test Organization
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Complex feature testing", "[Feature]") {
    // Common setup code
    SomeObject obj;
    
    SECTION("First scenario") {
        // Specific test case
        REQUIRE(obj.method1() == expected_value);
    }
    
    SECTION("Second scenario") {
        // Another test case with same setup
        REQUIRE(obj.method2() == other_expected);
    }
}

## Common Pitfalls and Solutions

### Floating-Point Comparisons

> **CRITICAL**: Never use Approx - it's deprecated due to asymmetry and other issues

❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
REQUIRE(calculated_volume == expected_volume);           // Exact equality
REQUIRE(calculated_volume == Catch::Approx(expected));   // Deprecated! Asymmetric!
```

✅ **Correct**: Always use floating point matchers
```cpp
// Absolute tolerance - good when values are near zero
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinAbs(expected_volume, 0.001));

// Relative tolerance - good for values with different magnitudes
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinRel(expected_volume, 0.01));  // 1% tolerance

// ULP (Units in Last Place) - most precise, requires IEEE-754
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinULP(expected_volume, 4));

// Combined approach - relative OR absolute
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, 
    WithinRel(expected_volume, 0.001) || WithinAbs(0.0, 0.000001));

// Precision control for output
Catch::StringMaker<double>::precision = 15;  // Show more decimal places
```

### Why Approx is Problematic:
- **Asymmetric**: `Approx(10).epsilon(0.1) != 11.1` but `Approx(11.1).epsilon(0.1) == 10`
- **Double-only**: All computation done in `double`, causes issues with `float` inputs  
- **Default behavior**: Only uses relative comparison, so `Approx(0) == X` only works for `X == 0`

### Path Handling
❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
std::string path = TEST_DATA_DIR + "/model.obj";  // May have path separator issues
```

✅ **Correct**:
```cpp
std::string path = std::string(TEST_DATA_DIR) + "/model.obj";
// or use boost::filesystem for complex path operations
```

### Exception Testing
❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
bool threw_exception = false;
try {
    risky_function();
} catch (...) {
    threw_exception = true;
}
REQUIRE(threw_exception);
```

✅ **Correct**:
```cpp
REQUIRE_THROWS(risky_function());
// or for specific exceptions
REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(risky_function(), SpecificException);
```

### Thread Safety

⚠️ **CRITICAL**: Catch2 assertions are **NOT thread-safe** by default!

> **Note**: Catch2 v3.9.0+ has opt-in thread-safe assertions via `CATCH_CONFIG_EXPERIMENTAL_THREAD_SAFE_ASSERTIONS`. OrcaSlicer is on v3.11.0 but does not enable this flag, so assertions remain non-thread-safe by default.

❌ **Incorrect**: Will cause undefined behavior or crashes
```cpp
std::thread t([&]() {
    REQUIRE(threaded_operation() == expected);  // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
    CHECK(other_operation());                   // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
});
```

✅ **Correct**: Collect results, assert on main thread
```cpp
std::atomic<bool> success{false};
std::atomic<int> error_count{0};

std::thread t([&]() {
    // Do work in thread, collect results
    bool result1 = (threaded_operation() == expected);
    bool result2 = other_operation();
    
    if (result1 && result2) {
        success = true;
    } else {
        error_count++;
    }
});

t.join();

// Assert results on main thread
REQUIRE(success);
REQUIRE(error_count == 0);
```

#### Thread Safety Rules:
- **REQUIRE family**: Would terminate process in spawned threads (throws exception with no try-catch)
- **CHECK family**: Not thread-safe, can corrupt internal state
- **SKIP, FAIL, SUCCEED**: Not thread-safe even with v3 thread-safe assertions
- **Message macros**: INFO, CAPTURE, WARN - not thread-safe
- **STATIC_REQUIRE/CHECK**: Not thread-safe (relies on runtime registration)

## Start with an eval failure

The fact that OrcaSlicer has a menu item or a config key is not a reason to add a tool. Start from a transcript or an automated eval in which the Agent cannot finish a real user task, finishes it only some of the time, or needs an unreasonable number of steps or tokens.

Write down:

- what the user wanted to achieve;
- the exact point where the current tools stop being enough;
- which OrcaSlicer state or operation is missing;
- what a successful transcript should look like;
- the unsafe or ambiguous cases that must fail; and
- the evidence that will show the new tool fixed the problem.

If the failure can be fixed by a clearer description, a better result, or a more useful validation error, improve the existing definition instead of adding a tool.

The candidate catalog later in this guide lists tools we might build. Being listed there does not accept a tool, and it does not excuse a tool from this section. A row in that catalog does two jobs. It records which product screen and which group of evals the tool would serve, which makes the eval easier to write. It also settles what the tool acts on, its action class, and its OrcaSlicer owner, so that two people do not build the same capability twice under different names.

----
### A reason travels with every refusal and every empty result

Added 2026-11-01, narrowed 2026-11-02. On 2026-10-31 a Bambu Lab P1S failed to connect through the printer chat: the person gave its address, the app had heard the printer in cloud mode, and the result said "No printer in LAN mode is on the network now". The right next step, turning LAN Only on, was in the app's hands and in nobody else's. The four rules above are about the code; this one is about the person on the other side of the model:

**A refusal or an empty result is wrong when it leaves a person stuck: told something false or useless at that moment, with the right next step hidden, at a cost beyond one more tool call.**

That is the whole test, and it is applied per case, not per code shape. A sweep on 2026-11-01 found eleven places where a result said less than the app knew. Judged by this test, three were real and were fixed; the other eight were not, and their fixes were taken out again (Kenneth, 2026-11-02: "fixing a non-problem is a lot worse than not fixing a real problem"). The model recovering the truth with its next ordinary call (`slice_report` after a bare `valid: false`, a search without a scope after an empty page) is not a stuck person, and every field added for such a case is text every model reads on every call. The three that were real:

1. **A wrong Bambu access code.** Upstream's handler erases the saved code and clears the selection; a backend that read the selection said "The selected printer changed" or "The printer is no longer available", and the person, who had mistyped the code from the printer's screen, was sent to refresh a list. `Printers/ConnectionEvents` records the plug-in's answer at the moment it arrives, and the backend reads that before it reads the selection.
2. **A print host that answered.** A Klipper owner who types the Mainsail port instead of Moonraker's, or picks Moonraker for an OctoPrint host, was told "Could not reach the print host. Check its address, API key and network." The host was reached and said what it was. One line of the host's own answer travels with the failure.
3. **A heard printer the connection does not offer.** A person retrying after a failed add, with the printer's serial already linked to the first saved entry, was told "no printer of this model is on the network" while it was being heard. Every printer the search heard is in `seen` with a `reason` (`other_model`, `linked_elsewhere`, `other_device`, `occupied`, `cloud_mode`, `account_only`), and the refusal names it.

What they share: the fork read what OrcaSlicer's event left behind (a cleared selection, a pass-or-fail flag, a filtered list) instead of the event itself, and the fakes could not produce the failing answer, so no test ever showed the sentence a person would read. The guard for a case that passes the test is a state table: arrange each state, read the tools that report it, and assert the results differ (`tests/agent/test_printer_conversation.cpp` "reports every printer it heard", the `--printer-setup` harness checks named `*_are_told_apart`), with the fake taught to produce every failure the real owner can (`FakeBambuAgent::fail_next_connect`, the harness's `StandInHost` with a status and body). Where a table deliberately leaves two states reading the same, a one-line comment at that assertion says why. Kenneth's rule of 2026-10-15 stands as it was: a rare failure the app has nothing more to say about gets one generic error.

### How to fix a result that hides the failure

Added 2026-11-02. The fix is mechanical, and a new check is almost never part of it. Four rules, in order (Kenneth, 2026-11-02):

1. **The source gives an error: forward it.** Pass on the `what()`, the reason string or the list the code already holds, and keep any instruction the sentence carried, such as "Do not repeat the call".
2. **The source gives nothing: say what the code tested or saw, and delete any guessed cause.** Do not add a check or a branch to tell causes apart. If the code does not know something, the sentence stops claiming it, and there is nothing further to investigate.
3. **A comment says a lower layer's message misleads the model: keep the replacement.** `generate_calibration` drops the load report on purpose, because the over-the-build-volume warning is about the test model before the generator cut it. A replacement with no such comment is not protected by this rule.
4. **The fix needs a file OrcaSlicer owns: skip the entry.** Kenneth approves any upstream change one by one.

A forwarded error reaches the model, so it must not name Orca or OrcaSlicer, and `AgentUI/src/wording.test.ts` does not see those strings.

False successes are the exception to rule 1, because the source reports nothing. These OrcaSlicer calls do not say when they failed, so check the outcome yourself:

- `store_stl` always returns true. `TriangleMesh::write_binary` returns false only when the file will not open, so a full disk shows only in the file size (84 + 50 per facet).
- `PresetBundle::export_current_configs` lists a file whether or not it was written.
- `Plater::split_object` returns nothing and only shows a dialog, and the model is unchanged.
- `ModelObject::split` splits a multi-volume object only by volume, so one solid part with a modifier stays whole however many shells it has.
