# Writing a connection skill

Draft of 2026-11-04 for Kenneth's review. Nothing here is agreed yet. Where a sentence describes code or a test, it describes what is on `jusprin-newui` at e27c962864; where it proposes a rule, it says so.

A connection skill is the text the app adds to a printer chat when a person tries to connect a printer of one connection type: `AgentUI/src/skills/connect-bambu/SKILL.md`, `connect-moonraker` and `connect-octoprint`. Read this before writing a new one or changing one. The general rules for skills, and for when a skill becomes a tool, are in [Tool extension guide, Skills versus tools](mcp-tool-extension-guide.md#skills-versus-tools); this document adds only what connecting a printer needs.

## What the skill is for

Kenneth's test, 2026-11-02: the skill is good if the agent guides a person who is stuck and makes educated guesses it labels as guesses, until the printer is connected or the person chooses to leave it. It is not judged by whether a printer connected, by how many states it names, or by whether every sentence in it is true. A skill that is never wrong and never helps a stuck person fails the test.

Three times in three days a skill was written to the wrong half of that test. The first Bambu skill was a table from state to next step, and on the real P1S it told a person with the right access code to re-check it. The second Bambu skill said "add no cause of your own", and the model repeated a false reason instead of guessing. The host skills said "you have not seen where Mainsail or Fluidd show the key", and on 2026-11-04 the model told a person who had no key to look in "Mainsail's settings page", which does not show it. Each time the writer kept "say nothing false" and dropped "help the stuck person".

## How the skill reaches the model

Facts about the code today.

- The app chooses the skill from the connection type and adds it to the conversation once, with the result of the first `printer_connection_status` or `printer_connect` call, or on the first request of a chat opened to connect (`PrinterConversation::connection_skill`, `AgentHost::session_skill`). The model never picks it. For a print host the type is known only from the first `printer_connect`'s `hostType` or a saved connection, so a host skill never arrives before the model has asked for an address and called connect.
- The skill stays in the chat once sent (`AgentSkillUse::stays`).
- Everything before that call runs on the standing prompt alone (`AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts`): the offer to connect after adding, the request for an address, the first connect call. A skill cannot guide those turns.
- The skill opens with "The rules above still apply", so wherever the standing prompt gives an exact sentence or an exact step, the prompt wins over a fact in the skill. On 2026-11-04 the prompt's finishing example "It is connected, so you can send prints straight to it" beat the skill's "verified means Moonraker answered, and nothing more", with Klipper shut down.

## Before writing: three audits

### 1. The person's stuck moments, not the app's states

Start from the moments a person with this connection type gets stuck, and write to those. The failure table (which error text means which step) comes second. The three moments every connection type has:

- **Giving the address.** What do they open in a browser, which port, what if the name does not resolve. For a host, this moment happens before the skill arrives, so what the person needs here belongs in the standing prompt or the skill's trigger has to move.
- **Being asked for a credential they do not have.** A Klipper owner who has never heard of an API key; a Bambu owner who cannot find the access code. The skill says, in order of cost to check, what is likeliest and what they can look at, each labelled as observed, documented or a guess. The 401-without-a-key case was the one place both 2026-11-04 runs got stuck, and the skill had only "search for where their version shows it".
- **Being told it is connected.** What "verified" proved and did not prove, so the closing sentence does not promise what the app has not checked.

For each moment, write what a competent friend would say to someone standing at that screen. That sentence is the skill's job; the error table supports it.

### 2. Information against knowledge, per state

Kenneth, 2026-11-02: for each failure, is the cause a lack or wrong *information* (a fact about this situation that only the app can know at that moment) or a lack or wrong *knowledge* (how things work)? Information belongs in the app's note or tool result; knowledge about connecting belongs in the skill; how to work in general belongs in the prompt.

Before writing a line of the skill, list the app's notes for this connection type and, for each, what the app knows at that moment that the model would need. Where the note lacks it, the fix is to the note, and the skill is written against the note that will exist. Examples found on 2026-11-04 for Moonraker:

- The failure note after HTTP 401 does not say whether the form was submitted empty or with a key, although `PrinterConversation::connect` holds the credential string. The model told a person who typed nothing that "it rejected the key".
- The verified note carries no Klipper state, although `Moonraker::test` reads `klippy_state` from `/server/info` and only logs it. The model said "you can send prints straight to it" to a printer whose Klipper was shut down.

The Bambu note was enriched after the 2026-11-02 incident (the plug-in's code, how long it took, a TCP look at port 8883 before and after). That fix was made once and never made a rule; this audit is the rule. Proposed.

### 3. The standing prompt and the tool descriptions

List every sentence in `printerInstructions.ts` and in the connection tools' descriptions (`Agent/ToolRegistry.cpp`) that gives an exact wording, an exact step or a procedure for connecting. Each one either goes, becomes conditional, or is accepted knowing the skill cannot override it. On 2026-11-04 three such sentences caused failures the skill's facts should have prevented: the "offer it once … with exactly" sentence after `printer_add` (asked a person who had already asked to connect), "say briefly to use that form" after `credential_requested` (told a person with no key to type one), and the finishing example above. The connect tool's "until they give one, ask for it instead of calling this" made the model ask permission to try a port the person had just said to try.

This matches [Tool extension guide, A tool description versus a skill](mcp-tool-extension-guide.md#skills-versus-tools): a description that has grown into a step belongs in the skill. The skill work added new text and never swept the old. Proposed as a required step.

## Writing the skill

### Explain the mechanism as a chain

Number the steps the connection goes through, each depending on the one before, and say so: a step that worked says nothing about the ones after it. This is what let Sonnet 5.5 reason about failures the skill did not list on 2026-11-03 (an OctoPrint the person called Klipper; `https://` against a plain-http host). Keep the chain from the person's side as well as the app's: for Moonraker, the app reaches Moonraker at its port, and so does the person's browser, so Moonraker's own pages, the key page included, are at that same address and port. The 2026-11-04 skill explained only the app's side, and the model sent the person to a port-80 URL for the key.

### Three kinds of statement, each labelled

- **Observed on a real host or printer.** What the app's own test reported, and when (the guard tests in `tests/agent/test_printer_conversation.cpp` require every state the skill names to have a dated run behind it). Write these as facts.
- **Documented.** What a maintainer's docs or FAQ say, named ("Moonraker's docs say…", "Mainsail's FAQ for this error says…"). Write these with their source. The evidence rule does not forbid them; leaving them out is what made the host skills silent about the one thing a stuck Klipper owner needs (that a 401 from a printer on the same home network is usually fixed in `trusted_clients`, with no key at all).
- **A guess.** General knowledge nobody has checked on this setup. Write it as a guess and give the cheapest check.

What not to write, each from an incident:

- One next step per state. The state-to-step table sent a person with the right code to re-check it (P1S, 2026-11-02).
- "Add no cause of your own" or anything that forbids reasoning. The model repeated a false reason (P1S, 2026-11-02). The guard bans the phrase.
- A menu path as fact (`Settings > WLAN`). The guard bans arrows and "Settings >".
- A menu path as a presupposition. "Search for where Mainsail shows the key" presupposes it does; the model filled it in with "Mainsail's settings page" (2026-11-04). Say what is known instead: Mainsail and Fluidd do not show it; the two ways to get it; when it is not needed.
- A sentence the standing prompt contradicts with an exact wording. The prompt wins; see audit 3.
- A fix as the single answer. "Restart the printer" became every chat's advice once it was the only untested suggestion listed (P1S, 2026-11-02).

### Search: say what to look up and how to read it

Every chat has the provider's web search. Two things are known about it. Offered with no instruction, the model did not search once in four chats (2026-11-02). Told to search before guessing, it searched in two of seven chats and cited its source (2026-11-03). Told to search for the key, it found Moonraker's docs, which give the key page without a port, and handed the person a wrong URL (2026-11-04).

So the skill names the search for each stuck moment and says how to apply the result to this setup: what the docs assume (Moonraker's default port), what varies by version, and what the model should ask the person to confirm. "Search before you say" alone was not enough.

### The length

The skill is read on every request after it arrives. The three skills today are 50 to 60 lines. A stuck-moment section for the credential adds a paragraph, not a page.

## The app's part

The skill is only as good as the notes it reads. For each connection type, the notes carry what audit 2 found (proposed; the Bambu note does this today, the host notes do not):

- A failed connection: the host's own words, forwarded unchanged ([How to fix a result that hides the failure](mcp-tool-extension-guide.md#how-to-fix-a-result-that-hides-the-failure)), plus what the app itself did and saw: whether a credential was sent, how long the test waited, what a port answered.
- A verified connection: what the app checked and anything it read on the way that bears on the next step, such as Klipper's state.
- The report card: today it is shown at exactly the second failure in a chat (`PrinterConversation::connection_failed`). A 401 after a wrong-port failure counted as the second failure on 2026-11-04 although it was progress. Whether the rule should count repeats of the same outcome instead is open.

## Testing a connection skill

### Offline, today

- `tests/agent/test_printer_conversation.cpp`: the skill arrives only once the type is known and never in a chat that only adds a printer; every state named in backquotes has a dated real run; banned phrases are absent.
- `AgentUI/src/skills.test.ts` and `wording.test.ts`: the file parses, the trigger is unique, the text says "the app" and never "arrives".
- The shell harness's `--print-host-check` and `--printer-connect-live-check`: the app's own test against a real host or printer, no model, the source of every "observed" line.

These prove where the skill arrives and that its facts were seen. They say nothing about whether its words help.

### Live, with Kenneth's test

The 2026-11-03 host chats ran Sonnet 5.5 against Docker hosts with a scripted person who had the key, took the port advice, and knew it was OctoPrint. All seven connected and nothing was learned about guidance. The 2026-11-04 chats ran GPT-5.4 Mini with a person who did not know what an API key was, and failed at every stuck moment.

So a live run of a connection skill (proposed):

- scripts a person who does **not** have the answer at each stuck moment: no key and no idea what one is; the Mainsail port; a `.local` name; Klipper shut down; the wrong host type;
- runs on the weakest model the product offers by default, not only on the model the writer prefers;
- is judged by where the person ends up (`ended_badly` in `tests/printer_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py`), including the closing sentence, not by whether the printer connected;
- reads the transcript as the model saw it, every tool call, result and note in order, before any line of the skill is changed, and names for each failure the text the model saw or lacked.

Live runs cost money and need Kenneth's approval of a specific batch with a token estimate.

## Checklist before a connection skill is committed

1. The three stuck moments are written to, each with labelled guesses in order of cost.
2. Audit 2 is written down: for each note, what the app knows and what the note says; the gaps are fixed or listed.
3. Audit 3 is written down: every exact connecting sentence in the prompt and the tool descriptions, and what was done with it.
4. Every state in backquotes has a dated real run; the guard passes.
5. Every documented claim names its source; every guess says it is one; no menu is stated or presupposed.
6. Each search the skill asks for says what to search and how to apply the answer.
7. A stuck-person live run on the default model, approved and run, with the transcript read before any edit.

## Where the rules come from

- 2026-10-31, P1S: the app hid a cloud-mode printer and the model invented menus. Tools report what the app saw.
- 2026-11-01: "a general process that improves when more people are using it" (Kenneth); tool results carry what is true now, a skill carries how it works.
- 2026-11-02: the state-to-step table failed on the real P1S; "guide the user… make educated guess"; "the goal here is not to connect my printer"; information against knowledge, and where each belongs.
- 2026-11-02 to 03: web search alone was never used; told to search, the model did, in some chats.
- 2026-11-03: the host skills were written from Docker evidence and proven with a person who knew the answers; "apply the lessons" was done from memory, and search was left out of them by mistake.
- 2026-11-04: two live Moonraker runs on GPT-5.4 Mini failed at each stuck moment. Diagnosis and lessons review in the side-session notes of 2026-11-04 (`moonraker-skill-diagnosis.md`, `connection-skill-lessons-review.md`).

2. Audit 2 is written down: for each note, what the app knows and what the note says; the gaps are fixed or listed.
3. Audit 3 is written down: every exact connecting sentence in the prompt and the tool descriptions, and what was done with it.
4. Every state in backquotes has a dated real run; the guard passes.
5. Every documented claim names its source; every guess says it is one; no menu is stated or presupposed.
6. Each search the skill asks for says what to search and how to apply the answer.
7. A stuck-person live run on the default model, approved and run, with the transcript read before any edit.

## Where the rules come from

- 2026-10-31, P1S: the app hid a cloud-mode printer and the model invented menus. Tools report what the app saw.
- 2026-11-01: "a general process that improves when more people are using it" (Kenneth); tool results carry what is true now, a skill carries how it works.
- 2026-11-02: the state-to-step table failed on the real P1S; "guide the user… make educated guess"; "the goal here is not to connect my printer"; information against knowledge, and where each belongs.
- 2026-11-02 to 03: web search alone was never used; told to search, the model did, in some chats.
- 2026-11-03: the host skills were written from Docker evidence and proven with a person who knew the answers; "apply the lessons" was done from memory, and search was left out of them by mistake.
- 2026-11-04: two live Moonraker runs on GPT-5.4 Mini failed at each stuck moment. Diagnosis and lessons review in the side-session notes of 2026-11-04 (`moonraker-skill-diagnosis.md`, `connection-skill-lessons-review.md`).

- `slice-failed` (trigger `slice_failed`): a plate's last slice did not succeed, because OrcaSlicer's check refused the plate or the run failed. The adapter records why on the plate (`WorkspacePlate::slice_failure`: refused or failed, OrcaSlicer's words, the setting and object when named) at the moment it happens (a hook in `Plater::reslice`, `Workspace/SliceRequests.hpp`, and the run's completion event), worded by the print-issue monitor's `slice_failure_of`, and keeps it until the plate slices. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceFailure`; `slice_report` of an unsliced plate adds the check code and the object's name. The skill fires once per failure, on the first request that carries it: the result of the model's own `slice_start`, the turn the app starts when a slice the model started fails after its turn, or the next message after the person's Slice all. The same refusal again is the same failure.

- `print-issues` (trigger `print_issues`): what the print-issue chip's Ask AI button asks for and how to read what OrcaSlicer reports. The adapter reads a slice's warnings through the monitor's `slice_warnings_of` while the plate is active and keeps a summary on the plate while that slice is current (`WorkspacePlate::slice_warnings`: the count, how many the person ignored, and the first warning, critical first, in OrcaSlicer's words with its setting and object). It counts every warning the chip lists. The chip and `slice_report` read the same slice-result rule (`Workspace/SliceResultWarnings`), so they list the same warnings, except that `slice_report` also lists the timelapse ones, marked `appliesWhen: "timelapse"`, which the chip does not count. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceWarnings`. The skill fires on the request that carries a chip's message, and on the first request whose workspace shows warnings no request has carried yet, whether the person sliced (their next message) or the model did (the tool result that shows them, or the app's turn when its slice ended after its turn); a re-slice with the same warnings fires nothing.
+The connection skills (`connect-bambu`, `connect-moonraker`, `connect-octoprint`) have rules of their own, in [Writing a connection skill](connection-skill-guide.md) (draft, under review).
The cases in between:

- **A procedure made of existing tool calls.** It is a skill for as long as carrying it out takes judgement. It becomes a tool only when the steps are fixed and the person wants the whole thing as one action that can be undone. If there are many such fixed sequences, they go in one workflow registry (see [When resources or skills are appropriate](#when-resources-or-skills-are-appropriate)).

The testing section separates the offline guards that exist from a live run with a scripted person who does not have the answer, on the weakest default model, judged by where they end up. It closes with a seven-item checklist and the dated incidents each rule comes from.

**What is marked as proposal.** The two note requirements (credential state after a failure, Klipper state after verify), the prompt sweep as a required step, the stuck-person live run, and reconsidering the second-failure rule for the report card. Mostly the first, and I should say so plainly.

**What the draft actually does.** Its rules are induced from the eight failures of 11-04 and the three of 11-02. The "what not to write" list is one incident per bullet. The three audits are the three places those incidents happened to land, dressed as a method. The stuck moments are the moments our two runs got stuck at. That is aggregation. A fourth connection type written from this guide would inherit rules shaped by what Moonraker and the P1S did wrong, and nothing in the guide tells its writer what helping requires in general.

**What the why-first version would start from.** The question is: at each point where the agent failed to help, what did it lack that a helpful person at that screen would have had? Reading the transcripts that way, the agent lacked one of four things each time, and none of them is specific to Moonraker:

1. **The person's situation.** Whether they had typed a key, whether Klipper was running. The app knew and the note did not say. A skill cannot supply this, but it can tell the model what the app does not tell it, so the model asks instead of assuming.
2. **The mechanism from the person's side.** The skill explained how the app reaches Moonraker and not how a person at a browser does, so the model could not apply the docs it found.
3. **A repertoire of ways out, ranked.** With one path, "the key page", the model concluded "not exposed that way" when it failed. A helpful person knows the three ways out of a 401 and which fits a home network.
4. **Consistent instructions.** The prompt's exact sentences contradicted the skill's facts, and the model obeyed the louder one.

From those four, what a connection skill must carry follows without reference to any incident: the chain from both sides, the person's and the app's; for each stuck moment, the ways out in order of likelihood with how to tell which applies; the questions to ask when the app's note is silent, and which facts the app cannot see at all; and nothing the standing prompt already decides. The incidents then become the evidence that each of those is needed, not the source of the rules.

The lessons review I wrote yesterday has the four lacks in its "why the lessons were not enough" section, so I had the material. When I wrote the guide I reached for the incident list because it was already in a table, and the table became the outline. The same thing the 11-02 memory note records: the writer kept what was easy to see and test.

# One live chat against the real P1S, 2026-11-01

Code under test: `claude/festive-lederberg-693438` (`ff2fee4fbd`, `ff10faa501`) plus the
scenario on `claude/printer-live-p1s`. Provider anthropic, model `claude-sonnet-5-5` as read
from the run's app config; the app's log does not record the model name in a request or
response, so that config line is the evidence. Printer: Bambu Lab P1S at 192.168.0.198,
cloud mode, not changed. Ran once, 09:01:48 to 09:02:46 PST.

## Verdict

The model told the truth about the printer and what to do. After the app's note it said the
P1S was found at 192.168.0.198 with LAN Only off, that it cannot connect as it is, that
LAN Only is turned on in the printer's network settings, and that connecting is optional.
It never said there is no printer on the network and gave no menu path.

Things to know:

- At +25 s, 6 seconds before the printer was heard, it said "The app didn't find your P1S on
  the network" after the app's 15-second note. True of what had been observed, but it does
  not say the search is still running, and it asked the person to go and look at the printer.
- It repeated the app's sentence that "the printer can prepare prints without a connection".
  The printer does not prepare prints; the app does. The wording comes from `kPersonsChoice` in
  PrinterConversation.cpp, so the model is faithful to a misleading line. "Network settings" also
  comes from the app's tool description; nobody checked it on the printer in this run.
- It never called `printer_connect`, so no model read the new refusal text in this run.
- The model did not ask for the address; the scenario volunteered it at +37 s.

## Checks

Five of six word and outcome checks passed. `live_p1s_words_invent_no_menu_path` failed on a false
positive: my word list had " menu" and the model said "Connect… in its menu on Home", a real app
menu named in printerInstructions.ts. The list was then narrowed; that narrowing has only been
compiled and checked against this saved transcript, since no second live chat is allowed.

Before the chat I ran the free `--printer-network-check` twice with this new binary. The first run,
about 08:57, heard nothing for 120 seconds while reporting search state `listening` and failed. A
plain Python listener at 09:00 heard three announcements in 45 seconds. The second run, just after,
heard the printer at 25 s and passed. Cause unknown. My hypothesis, unverified: macOS Local Network
permission on a new executable's first run.

# How printers announce: what is known, 2026-11-01

Withdrawn: my suggestion to wait 45 seconds. It rested on six timings and no search.

Official: Bambu's wiki lists device discovery on UDP 1990 and 2021, SSDP multicast or broadcast, in cloud and LAN mode. Seen only through a search result; fetching the page returned HTTP 402. I found no published timing.

Community, not official: one person captured a P1S in LAN mode sending every 5 seconds, destination toggling between 1990 and 2021, which would make 2021 every 10 seconds. One capture, on another network.

General: IETF documents say Wi-Fi multicast has no acknowledgement or retransmission. That packet loss causes our delays is a hypothesis, not tested.

Measured here: two announcements 9.9 s apart in a 30 s listen, first at 19.2 s. App first-heard times 14, 21, 25, 25, 40 s, plus 38 s on 2026-10-31, and one 120 s miss. A 10 s period does not explain those, so something else is at work; unknown what.

Void: a 10-minute listen from about 10:37 heard nothing because the Mac had moved to 192.168.15.221 after a clamshell sleep at 10:14. The 08:57 miss predates that sleep and stays unexplained.

Not measured yet: announcement gaps over a long listen; first-heard times over many no-model runs. Both are free and need the Mac on 192.168.0.x.

# How printers announce: what is known, 2026-11-01

Withdrawn: my suggestion to wait 45 seconds. It rested on six timings and no search.

Official: Bambu's wiki lists device discovery on UDP 1990 and 2021, SSDP multicast or broadcast, in cloud and LAN mode. Seen only through a search result; fetching the page returned HTTP 402. I found no published timing.

Community, not official: one person captured a P1S in LAN mode sending every 5 seconds, destination toggling between 1990 and 2021, which would make 2021 every 10 seconds. One capture, on another network.

General: IETF documents say Wi-Fi multicast has no acknowledgement or retransmission. That packet loss causes our delays is a hypothesis, not tested.

Measured here: two announcements 9.9 s apart in a 30 s listen, first at 19.2 s. App first-heard times 14, 21, 25, 25, 40 s, plus 38 s on 2026-10-31, and one 120 s miss. A 10 s period does not explain those, so something else is at work; unknown what.

Void: a 10-minute listen from about 10:37 heard nothing because the Mac had moved to 192.168.15.221 after a clamshell sleep at 10:14. The 08:57 miss predates that sleep and stays unexplained.

Not measured yet: announcement gaps over a long listen; first-heard times over many no-model runs. Both are free and need the Mac on 192.168.0.x.

# One live chat against the real P1S, 2026-11-01

Code under test: `claude/festive-lederberg-693438` (`ff2fee4fbd`, `ff10faa501`) plus the
scenario on `claude/printer-live-p1s`. Provider anthropic, model `claude-sonnet-5-5` as read
from the run's app config; the app's log does not record the model name in a request or
response, so that config line is the evidence. Printer: Bambu Lab P1S at 192.168.0.198,
cloud mode, not changed. Ran once, 09:01:48 to 09:02:46 PST.

## Verdict

The model told the truth about the printer and what to do. After the app's note it said the
P1S was found at 192.168.0.198 with LAN Only off, that it cannot connect as it is, that
LAN Only is turned on in the printer's network settings, and that connecting is optional.
It never said there is no printer on the network and gave no menu path.

Things to know:

- At +25 s, 6 seconds before the printer was heard, it said "The app didn't find your P1S on
  the network" after the app's 15-second note. True of what had been observed, but it does
  not say the search is still running, and it asked the person to go and look at the printer.
- It repeated the app's sentence that "the printer can prepare prints without a connection".
  The printer does not prepare prints; the app does. The wording comes from `kPersonsChoice` in
  PrinterConversation.cpp, so the model is faithful to a misleading line. "Network settings" also
  comes from the app's tool description; nobody checked it on the printer in this run.
- It never called `printer_connect`, so no model read the new refusal text in this run.
- The model did not ask for the address; the scenario volunteered it at +37 s.

## Checks

Five of six word and outcome checks passed. `live_p1s_words_invent_no_menu_path` failed on a false
positive: my word list had " menu" and the model said "Connect… in its menu on Home", a real app
menu named in printerInstructions.ts. The list was then narrowed; that narrowing has only been
compiled and checked against this saved transcript, since no second live chat is allowed.

## The first no-model check missed the printer

Before the chat I ran the free `--printer-network-check` twice with this new binary. The first run,
about 08:57, heard nothing for 120 seconds while reporting search state `listening` and failed. A
plain Python listener at 09:00 heard three announcements in 45 seconds. The second run, just after,
heard the printer at 25 s and passed. Cause unknown. My hypothesis, unverified: macOS Local Network
permission on a new executable's first run.

# How printers announce: what is known, 2026-11-01

Withdrawn: my suggestion to wait 45 seconds. It rested on six timings and no search.

Official: Bambu's wiki lists device discovery on UDP 1990 and 2021, SSDP multicast or broadcast, in cloud and LAN mode. Seen only through a search result; fetching the page returned HTTP 402. I found no published timing.

Community, not official: one person captured a P1S in LAN mode sending every 5 seconds, destination toggling between 1990 and 2021, which would make 2021 every 10 seconds. One capture, on another network.

General: IETF documents say Wi-Fi multicast has no acknowledgement or retransmission. That packet loss causes our delays is a hypothesis, not tested.

Measured here: two announcements 9.9 s apart in a 30 s listen, first at 19.2 s. App first-heard times 14, 21, 25, 25, 40 s, plus 38 s on 2026-10-31, and one 120 s miss. A 10 s period does not explain those, so something else is at work; unknown what.

Void: a 10-minute listen from about 10:37 heard nothing because the Mac had moved to 192.168.15.221 after a clamshell sleep at 10:14. The 08:57 miss predates that sleep and stays unexplained.

Not measured yet: announcement gaps over a long listen; first-heard times over many no-model runs. Both are free and need the Mac on 192.168.0.x.

# Every failed connection scenario, 2026-10-31 to 11-04, one at a time

Written 2026-11-04. Each entry: the setup, what the model said (quoted from the transcript), what the model had been given, and what went wrong in that scenario alone. "Verified" means I read the text the model saw; "inferred" means the cause is my reading of it. No patterns drawn here on purpose.

Sources: Kenneth's paste of the 10-31 chat; `p1s-live-chat-2026-11-01.md`; the harness logs recorded in the implement session's transcript (11-02, 11-03); `wrong-code-search.log` and `no-printer-search.log` (11-02 web-search experiment); the two 11-04 transcripts. Two scripted-suite cases (D2, D4) I have only through the agent's report.

---

## A. 2026-10-31. Kenneth's P1S, cloud mode. The shipped app, no skill, no tool fix. Model: the app's configured one (not recorded).

**A1. Asked for an address for a Bambu printer.** After the plug-in installed, the app's note said "Bambu's network plug-in is installed now, so Bambu Lab P1S can be connected." The model: "I need the printer's address — the same one you open in a browser." The prompt said to call `printer_connection_status` for a Bambu printer. The note said the printer could be connected and nothing about what to do next; the generic connect route in the prompt was "ask for the address". Verified that the note led nowhere; that this is why the model took the host route is inferred.

**A2. Menu steps from nowhere.** "On the printer screen, tap the menu icon, then open Settings, then Network." Nothing the model had seen named any menu. The prompt said "say where to find any answer you ask for". Inferred: the rule demanded a location and the model supplied one from memory.

**A3. Three false refusals, three identical replies.** Kenneth gave 192.168.0.198. `printer_connect` answered "No printer in LAN mode is on the network now" although no search had started; the printer was then heard in cloud mode and the tool hid it. The model, three times: "It couldn't find the printer on the network right now. Try again with the same address, set up the connection manually in the app, or leave it for now." It mentioned "checking Bambu LAN mode" once, never saying it was required or that the printer had been seen. What went wrong: the tool result was false and hid the one fact that mattered (verified); the prompt forced the same three options after every failure, and "set up manually" named a path the printer chat does not have (verified from the 11-02 analysis of the prompt). The model had no fact to reason from and no permission to vary its answer.

## B. 2026-11-01. Same P1S, cloud mode. Tool fix in place (search state, `seen` with reasons), no skill. Sonnet 5.5, scripted person. Two chats; the connection outcome was right in both. Three wrong sentences:

**B1. "The app didn't find your P1S on the network", 6 s and 2 s before it was heard.** The model had the note "The network search has listened for 15 seconds and has found no printer of this model. The app posts another note if one appears." It treated the 15-second mark as a result and sent the person to the printer's screen. Nothing it had said how long a first announcement takes (8 to 40 s on this printer, measured later). Verified the note; the timing gap is what was missing.

**B2. "The search stops after about 15 seconds if nothing appears."** False. The tool description said the app posts a note after about 15 seconds with none. The model turned "a note at 15 s" into "stops at 15 s". Verified.

**B3. "The printer can prepare prints without a connection."** Repeated from the app's note word for word. The app prepares prints, not the printer. Wrong information from the app; fixed the same day. Verified.

## C. 2026-11-02, morning. First Bambu skill: a table from state to next step. Sonnet 5.5, real P1S, which was very slow that day (pings 35 to 64 percent lost). Scripted person.

**C1. Made-up code, twice: no new idea.** Note after the first failure: "Connection to Bambu Lab P1S failed: The printer refused the connection; Bambu's network plug-in reported code -1. Check that the printer is on and in LAN mode, then try again." Model: "The printer refused the connection. Please compare the access code on the printer's screen with the one you typed." After the second: "The printer refused the connection again, and the code doesn't say why. You can try once more, set up the connection manually in the app, or leave it for now." The skill's `failed` line said: "the app's note gives the reason; say it in one sentence and add no cause of your own. The plug-in's code -1 does not tell a wrong access code from no answer, so never say which it was. Ask them to compare the access code." So the model did exactly what it was told: one sentence, one action, no reasoning. The note's "refused" was itself unsupported (code -1 came with no device at the address too). Verified from the skill text and the log.

**C2. Right code: sent back to the code.** Same note, same skill line. Model: code -1 "doesn't say whether the access code was wrong or something else went wrong", then still told Kenneth to compare the code. The real cause, a login that took 28 s against a plug-in that gives up at 24 s, was invisible: the note carried only "code -1". The skill forbade a guess and prescribed the one check. Verified.

**C3. "Set up manually" every time.** The prompt's connecting rule told the model to offer it after each failure. The printer chat has no such path. The model could not explain what it meant when asked. Verified from the 11-02 analysis.

## D. 2026-11-02, evening. Rewritten Bambu skill: explains the chain, failure read from the port look. The note now reports the plug-in's code, the delay, and a TCP look at port 8883 before and after. Sonnet 5.5, same slow P1S.

**D1. Every failure led to "restart the printer".** Right-code chat, note: "code -1 22 seconds after being asked to connect … Just before the attempt, it answered in 239 ms. Right after it failed, nothing answered within 5 seconds." Model: "The printer answered just before the attempt and then went quiet, so I can't tell whether the code was wrong. My guess is that the printer is slow to respond to logins. … The easiest thing to try is to turn the printer off and on." Told the code was the same: "Then the code is probably not the problem. … The most useful thing to try is to restart the printer." Good reasoning; but in the made-up-code chat the same skill never had it suggest re-checking the code, the cheapest check. The skill said "waiting several minutes or restarting the printer comes before trying again", an untested suggestion written as the step. The writer's own words: "the restart line is the same mistake repeated: I removed 'compare the code' and wrote a new single answer in its place." Verified.

**D2. No printer heard: only waits.** Scripted suite, DeepSeek V4 Flash, case `connect-bambu-not-found`: 5 of 5 on the old skill, 0 of 3 on the new. "In every run the model said it was still listening and would wait, and gave nothing to check" (commit c56ad86be2). The old skill's `listening` line said "ask what the printer's own screen shows about its connection"; the rewrite dropped it and said for `started` "say you are looking and end your message", with nothing for the moment the 15-second note arrives empty. Reported by the agent; I did not read these transcripts. Kenneth had the case removed.

**D3. "One candidate, and they asked to connect, so connect."** Appeared as a chat message in every chat. Text the model wrote beside a tool call reached the person. Cause never traced. Verified that it appeared.

**D4. DeepSeek stated "Settings > LAN" as fact; Sonnet did not.** Scripted suite. Reported by the agent. Same pressure as A2 plus a weaker model.

**D5. "Have you restarted it since this happened?"** asked seconds after suggesting the restart. Minor; verified in the log.

## E. 2026-11-02, evening. Web search only, no skill. Sonnet 5.5, P1S restarted and healthy (port 8883 in 10 to 123 ms). Four chats.

**E1. Never searched.** The search tool was offered in every request (the cached prompt grew by its 2,500 tokens); zero searches in four chats. The prompt said nothing about using it. Verified from the search log.

**E2. No printer heard: "my next guess is that the printer isn't in LAN mode."** After ruling out off, other Wi-Fi, guest network, VPN. Wrong: a printer with LAN Only off is still heard, and the app reports it as cloud mode. That fact is about this app's behaviour; only the skill states it, and no web search would find it. Verified.

**E3. "You can find it on the printer's screen in the network settings"** stated as fact for the access code, twice; in the first chat the same claim was labelled a guess. Model's own knowledge, unverified, inconsistent labelling. Verified.

(The wrong-code chat here was not a failure: "My guess is a small typo, or the code on the printer has changed", then after the second refusal "My new guess is that the printer I found isn't yours", with a cheap check. The note that time said "The printer refused the access code", and the printer was healthy.)

## F. 2026-11-03. Host skills, Moonraker and OctoPrint in Docker, Sonnet 5.5, with search. Scripted person who had the key and took advice. Six of seven connected.

**F1. Chat 5, `https://` timeout, not connected.** Model's first guess was right: "My guess is the `https://` at the start." The script answered a different question ("Both are on the same network. What else could it be?"), the model moved to a second guess (127.0.0.1 means this computer), the script said "OK, try that" with no address, the model asked for one, the script said "Thanks!". The script's fault. One thing to note: when the person answered beside the point, the model let its correct first guess drop instead of saying "the https is still my first suspect; let's try http before anything else". Verified.

**F2. Chat 6, "The printer also reports nothing loaded right now."** The prompt said "Loaded, as the printer reports it: nothing" for any connected printer; a Moonraker connection reports nothing about filament. Wrong information from the prompt; fixed 11-03. Verified.

**F3. Chat 6 rerun, "Mainsail's address is saved"** before the check ran. The app saves the address only when verified. Nothing told the model when saving happens; it inferred from the tool's success. Verified.

**F4. Chat 1, 401 with no key: the right URL, by luck of the input.** The person said "Moonraker is at http://127.0.0.1:7125". The model: "Open http://127.0.0.1:7125/access/api_key." Correct. The same skill on 11-04 produced a port-80 URL, because there the person had given the Mainsail address and the model had derived 7125 itself; the docs it found give the page without a port. So in this scenario the skill did not teach the model where Moonraker's pages live; the person's input carried the port. Verified in both logs.

**F5. Chat 1, the raw traceback.** The failure note showed Moonraker's 401 JSON with a Python traceback to the person. The host's words forwarded unchanged, as the rule says, and too much of them. Verified.

## G. 2026-11-04. Moonraker in Docker on Kenneth's Mac: port 7125 needs a key, Mainsail on 8081 does not pass requests on. GPT-5.4 Mini via OpenRouter. Person: a Voron owner who does not know what an API key is. Connected after five turns. Full diagnosis in `moonraker-skill-diagnosis.md`; the scenario-level facts:

**G1. "Want to connect it so you can send prints straight to it?"** after "I want to connect it so I can send prints to it." The prompt orders that sentence, with "exactly", after every successful `printer_add`. The skill was not yet in the chat. Verified.

**G2. "Please type it there"** for a person with no key, at the first `credential_requested`. The skill had just arrived with the result and says "The field can stay empty"; the prompt says "say briefly to use that form". The model followed the prompt. Verified.

**G3. "If you want, I can try that address now"** after "can you just try it?". The 7125 address was the model's guess; the connect tool's description says to pass only an address the person gave, and the conduct rule says to ask before connecting on a guess. Inferred.

**G4. "It rejected the key"** after a 401 with the form submitted empty. The note did not say whether a key was sent; the model's own prior "type it there" set its belief. Note lacks the fact: verified. Link: inferred.

**G5. `http://192.168.0.171/access/api_key`, then "the key isn't exposed that way".** The model had just established 8081 is Mainsail and 7125 is Moonraker, searched, got Moonraker's docs (which give `http://{host}/access/api_key` with no port), and sent the person to port 80. When it failed it concluded the key page does not exist and, in the same turn, called `printer_connect` again with nothing changed. The skill never says Moonraker's own pages are at Moonraker's port. Docs verified; link inferred.

**G6. "Look for an API key or access page in Mainsail's settings"** with no search. The skill says "You have not seen where Mainsail or Fluidd show the key, so search for where their version shows it". Mainsail shows no such page (its 401 FAQ points to `trusted_clients`). The model filled the presupposition. Inferred; the absence of a Mainsail key page is from my search.

**G7. The report card after the second failure**, a 401 that was progress. The rule counts to two. Verified.

**G8. "It's connected now, so you can send prints straight to it"** with Klipper in error. The prompt's finishing example is that sentence; the skill's step 4 says verified means only that Moonraker answered; the note said only "verified". Verified.

## H. 2026-11-04. Kenneth's Pi at `http://raspberrypi.local/`, no key needed, Klipper shut down. GPT-5.4 Mini. Person: generic Klipper, 240 × 225 bed, BLTouch. Connected in three turns.

**H1. Called `printer_connect` before any printer was added** ("no_printer: add one first"), then asked "Which printer model is it?". Recovered in one turn. The person had said "connect it" in the first message and the prompt's adding rules were in force. Minor.

**H2. Redundant "Want to connect it?"** as G1.

**H3. "The field can be left blank or filled with the key from Mainsail's settings page."** Half right (blank), half the same presupposition as G6, with no search in this chat since the opening one. Verified.

**H4. "It's connected, so you can send prints straight to it"** with Klipper shut down; then, asked "is it ready to print right now?", correctly "I can't see the printer's current state from here, only that it's connected." The model knew the skill's fact and said the prompt's sentence first. Verified.

**H5. 250 × 250 bed kept.** The person said 240 × 225. In add mode the prompt has no word about bed size and no tool sets it; the printer list shows each entry's volume. Dropped silently. Verified.

# Every time the printer chat failed to help someone connect a printer, 31 October to 4 November 2026

Written 4 November 2026. This replaces an earlier version of the same file that used words of my own. Each run below is told as what happened, in order. For every failure I say what the AI had in front of it when it wrote the bad sentence, and what went wrong in that case alone. I draw no general conclusions here.

## Words this report uses

- **The printer chat**: the chat panel in JusPrin where a person adds a printer and can connect it. An AI model answers in it.
- **The AI's standing instructions**: the text the AI reads at the start of every printer chat. It is written in the file `printerInstructions.ts`. I will call it "the standing instructions".
- **The extra connection instructions**: a second text the app adds into the chat the first time the person tries to connect, chosen by the kind of connection (Bambu, Moonraker or OctoPrint). The code calls these files "skills"; I will say "the extra connection instructions". They begin with the sentence "The rules above still apply", so where the standing instructions and the extra instructions disagree, the standing instructions are meant to win.
- **Actions the AI can ask the app to perform**: for connecting there are two. "Check connection status" (the code calls it `printer_connection_status`) asks the app what it knows about the printer on the network. "Connect" (`printer_connect`) asks the app to open a small form on screen where the person types the access code or API key, and then to try the connection. The AI never sees what is typed in that form.
- **A message from the app**: a line the app itself writes into the chat for the AI to read, such as "Connection to Voron 2.4 350 failed: HTTP 401". The person did not type it and the AI did not write it.
- **Bambu access code**: the six characters a Bambu printer shows on its own screen; a program must present them to connect over the local network.
- **LAN Only mode**: a setting on a Bambu printer. When it is off, the printer talks to Bambu's cloud and JusPrin cannot connect to it. When it is on, JusPrin can connect directly. The code says "cloud mode" for off.
- **The printer's broadcast**: a Bambu printer sends a small packet onto the local network about every ten seconds saying, in effect, "I am a P1S at this address, LAN Only on or off". The app finds Bambu printers by listening for these; nobody types an address.
- **Bambu's network plug-in**: a closed-source library from Bambu that the app uses to talk to Bambu printers. When a connection fails it reports only a number, and the number was always -1 in these tests.
- **Moonraker, Mainsail, Klipper**: Klipper is firmware that runs a hobbyist printer. Moonraker is the program beside it that other programs talk to over the network, normally on port 7125. Mainsail (or Fluidd) is the web page people open in a browser to use the printer; it talks to Moonraker for them.
- **API key**: the long secret string Moonraker or OctoPrint can require from a program. Moonraker usually does not require one from a computer on the same home network.
- **OctoPrint**: another program that runs beside a printer and offers a web page; it always requires an API key.
- **The automated test program**: a program that starts the real JusPrin, opens the printer chat, and plays the person from a fixed list of lines ("say: Connect my printer", "type into the form: a wrong code"). I will say "the test program playing the person". It cannot react to what the AI says; it says its next line regardless.
- **The AI models**: Claude Sonnet 5.5 from Anthropic (the stronger model used in most live runs); DeepSeek V4 Flash (a cheaper model used in the automated test suite); GPT-5.4 Mini from OpenAI (a cheaper model used on 4 November).
- **Test printers in Docker**: on 3 and 4 November, Moonraker, Mainsail and OctoPrint were run as containers on Kenneth's Mac to stand in for real printers. They answer like the real programs but there is no printer behind them.

---

## Run 1. 31 October. Kenneth tries to connect his own P1S. The shipped app, before any fix.

Kenneth's P1S was on, with LAN Only off. There were no extra connection instructions yet, and the app had two bugs in what it told the AI.

**What happened.** Kenneth added the P1S and said "Connect it". The app said Bambu's network plug-in was not installed, and Kenneth installed it. The app then wrote into the chat: "Bambu's network plug-in is installed now, so Bambu Lab P1S can be connected." The AI replied: "Bambu Lab P1S can be connected now. I need the printer's address — the same one you open in a browser when you use it on your network." Kenneth asked how to find it; the AI said: "On the printer screen, tap the menu icon, then open Settings, then Network." Kenneth typed 192.168.0.198. The AI tried to connect and the app refused with "No printer in LAN mode is on the network now". The AI said: "It couldn't find the printer on the network right now. Try again with the same address, set up the connection manually in the app, or leave it for now." Kenneth said "try it again" and "try it now"; the AI gave the same three options twice more, once adding "after checking Bambu LAN mode on the printer". Kenneth never connected.

**What went wrong, piece by piece.**

1. *Asking for an address.* A Bambu printer is found by its broadcast, not by an address; the standing instructions said to check connection status for a Bambu printer. But the app's message said only that the printer "can be connected" and gave no next step, and the standing instructions' other route (for Moonraker and OctoPrint) is "ask for the address". My reading is that the AI took the generic route because the message pointed nowhere. I checked the message; the reason is my inference.

2. *Menu steps the AI invented.* Nothing the AI had read named any menu on the printer. The standing instructions said "say where to find any answer you ask for", so the AI had to name a location and supplied one from memory. Nobody checked whether those steps match a P1S.

3. *A false refusal, and the real fact hidden.* When the AI first tried to connect, the app had not even started listening for broadcasts, yet it said "no printer in LAN mode is on the network". Seven seconds before the last refusal the app had in fact heard the P1S, with LAN Only off, and deliberately kept it out of what the AI could see. So the AI had no way to say the one thing that would have helped: "your printer is there, but LAN Only is off on it; turn it on". The standing instructions also told the AI to offer the same three options after every failure, and one of them, "set up the connection manually in the app", is a path the printer chat does not have. The AI had no fact to reason from and no permission to say anything different. I verified both the hiding and the three forced options in the code and in the analysis made on 2 November.

## Run 2. 1 November. Same P1S, after the app was fixed to say what it heard. Sonnet 5.5. The test program played the person.

The app now tells the AI what the listening has found, including a printer heard with LAN Only off. Two chats were run. In both the AI got the outcome right: it said the P1S was at 192.168.0.198 with LAN Only off, that it could not connect as it was, and that connecting was optional. Three sentences were wrong.

1. *"The app didn't find your P1S on the network", said 6 seconds (and in the second chat 2 seconds) before the printer was heard.* The AI had just read the app's message: "The network search has listened for 15 seconds and has found no printer of this model. The app posts another note if one appears." It read "found nothing in 15 seconds" as a result and sent the person to look at the printer. On this P1S the first broadcast took between 8 and 40 seconds to arrive, and nothing the AI had read said so.

2. *"The search stops after about 15 seconds if nothing appears."* False; the app keeps listening. The description of the check-status action said the app posts a message after about 15 seconds with nothing found. The AI turned "a message at 15 seconds" into "stops at 15 seconds".

3. *"The printer can prepare prints without a connection."* The AI repeated the app's own message word for word. The app prepares prints, not the printer. Fixed the same day.

## Run 3. 2 November, morning. The first version of the extra connection instructions for Bambu. Sonnet 5.5. Kenneth's P1S, which was very slow that day (it lost a third to two thirds of pings). The test program played the person, and Kenneth typed his real code when asked.

The first version of the extra instructions was a list: for each thing the app can report, one line saying what to do. The line for a failed connection read: "the app's note gives the reason; say it in one sentence and add no cause of your own. The plug-in's code -1 does not tell a wrong access code from no answer, so never say which it was. Ask them to compare the access code on the printer's screen with what they typed."

1. *A deliberately wrong code, twice: no new idea.* The test program typed a random string as the code. The app's message: "Connection to Bambu Lab P1S failed: The printer refused the connection; Bambu's network plug-in reported code -1. Check that the printer is on and in LAN mode, then try again." The AI: "The printer refused the connection. Please compare the access code on the printer's screen with the one you typed." The test program said it had checked and typed the same wrong string again. The AI: "The printer refused the connection again, and the code doesn't say why. You can try once more, set up the connection manually in the app, or leave it for now." What went wrong: the AI did exactly what its one line told it to do, one sentence, one action, no reasoning. The app's word "refused" was itself unsupported: the plug-in gives the same -1 when there is no printer at the address at all. And the standing instructions still forced the three options including "set up manually".

2. *Kenneth's real code: sent back to check the code.* Same message from the app, same line in the instructions. The AI said code -1 "doesn't say whether the access code was wrong or something else went wrong", and then still told Kenneth to compare the code with the screen. The real cause was invisible to everyone: a direct login with the right code took 28 seconds on the slow printer, and the plug-in gives up after about 24. The app's message carried only "code -1", and the instructions forbade a guess.

## Run 4. 2 November, evening. The rewritten extra instructions for Bambu, which explain how the connection works instead of listing one step per report. Sonnet 5.5. Same slow P1S.

The app's failure message now also reports what the app saw at the printer's login port (8883) just before and just after the attempt.

1. *Every failure led to "restart the printer".* With Kenneth's real code the app's message was: "Bambu's network plug-in reported code -1 22 seconds after being asked to connect, which does not say why. The app also tried the printer's port 8883 at 192.168.0.198. Just before the attempt, it answered in 239 ms. Right after it failed, nothing answered within 5 seconds." The AI: "The printer answered just before the attempt and then went quiet, so I can't tell whether the code was wrong. My guess is that the printer is slow to respond to logins. A slow printer can fail even with the right code. … The easiest thing to try is to turn the printer off and on." Told the code was the same: "Then the code is probably not the problem." That part is good. But with a deliberately wrong code the same instructions never had the AI suggest looking at the code again, the cheapest thing to check. The rewritten instructions said "waiting several minutes or restarting the printer comes before trying again", a suggestion nobody had tested, written as the next step. The author's own words afterwards: "the restart line is the same mistake repeated: I removed 'compare the code' and wrote a new single answer in its place."

2. *No printer heard: the AI only waits.* In the automated suite, run with DeepSeek, the case where no printer is on the network passed 5 of 5 times with the first instructions and 0 of 3 with the rewrite. In every run the AI said it was still listening and would wait, and gave the person nothing to check. The first version had said, for that situation, "ask what the printer's own screen shows about its connection"; the rewrite dropped that and had nothing for the moment the app's 15-second message says nothing was found. I did not read these transcripts; this is from the author's report and the commit message. Kenneth later had the case removed from the suite.

3. *The AI's notes to itself appeared in the chat.* "One candidate, and they asked to connect, so connect." showed up as a chat message in every chat. Text the AI wrote beside its action request reached the person. The cause was never traced.

4. *DeepSeek stated "Settings > LAN" as fact; Sonnet did not.* From the automated suite, reported by the author. Same pressure as in run 1: the instructions ask for a location and the model names one.

## Run 5. 2 November, evening. Web search only, with the extra connection instructions removed on purpose. Sonnet 5.5. Kenneth had restarted the P1S and it was healthy.

The question was whether giving the AI a web search would replace the hand-written instructions. Four chats.

1. *The AI never searched.* The search tool was offered in every request and the AI used it zero times in four chats. Nothing told it to.

2. *No printer heard: a wrong guess only the instructions could have prevented.* The test program made the app ignore the printer's broadcasts. The AI guessed in turn: off, other Wi-Fi, guest network, VPN; then "My next guess is that the printer isn't in LAN mode." That is wrong for this app: a printer with LAN Only off is still heard, and the app reports it as such. That fact is about how JusPrin behaves, only the removed instructions state it, and no web search would find it.

3. *Where the access code is, stated as fact in one chat and as a guess in another.* "You can find it on the printer's screen in the network settings." Nothing the AI had read said where the code is shown.

The wrong-code chat in this run was fine: "My guess is a small typo, or the code on the printer has changed", then after the second failure "My new guess is that the printer I found isn't yours", with a cheap check.

## Run 6. 3 November. The new extra instructions for Moonraker and OctoPrint, with web search allowed. Sonnet 5.5. Test printers in Docker. The test program played a person who already had the API key and did what the AI suggested.

Seven chats; six ended connected, including the one where Moonraker demanded a key. The failures were small:

1. *The one that did not connect was the test program's fault.* The address was `https://127.0.0.1:7126` against a server that speaks plain `http`. The AI's first guess was right: "My guess is the `https://` at the start." The test program's next fixed line answered a different question ("Both are on the same network. What else could it be?"), so the AI moved to a second guess, then the program said "OK, try that" with no address, the AI asked for one, and the program said "Thanks!". One thing worth noticing: when the person answered beside the point, the AI let its correct first guess drop instead of saying "the https is still my first suspect".

2. *"The printer also reports nothing loaded right now."* The standing instructions told the AI, for any connected printer, "Loaded, as the printer reports it: nothing". A Moonraker connection reports nothing about filament at all. Wrong information from the app; fixed that day.

3. *"Mainsail's address is saved", said before the connection was checked.* The app saves the address only after a successful check. Nothing had told the AI when saving happens.

4. *The key page URL was right only because the person had typed Moonraker's port.* In the chat where Moonraker demanded a key, the person's opening line was "Moonraker is at http://127.0.0.1:7125". The AI said: "Open http://127.0.0.1:7125/access/api_key", which is correct. On 4 November the same instructions produced a wrong URL (next run), because there the person had given Mainsail's address and the AI had worked out port 7125 itself. So in this run the instructions did not teach the AI where Moonraker's pages live; the person's input carried the port.

5. *The app showed a raw error to the person.* The failure message included Moonraker's 401 answer with a Python stack trace.

## Run 7. 4 November. Moonraker in Docker on Kenneth's Mac: port 7125 requires a key, and the Mainsail page on port 8081 does not pass requests through. GPT-5.4 Mini. The person: a Voron owner who does not know what an API key is. Connected after five turns.

1. *"Want to connect it so you can send prints straight to it?"* asked after the person had opened with "I want to connect it so I can send prints to it." The standing instructions order that exact sentence after every successful add, with no exception. The extra connection instructions were not in the chat yet; they arrive only with the first connection attempt.

2. *"Please type it there"* to a person with no key, when the form opened. The extra instructions had just arrived and say "The field can stay empty"; the standing instructions say "say briefly to use that form". The AI followed the standing instructions.

3. *"If you want, I can try that address now"* after the person said "can you just try it?". Port 7125 was the AI's own guess. The description of the connect action says to pass only an address the person gave, and the standing instructions say to ask before acting on a guess. My inference.

4. *"Moonraker is there, but it rejected the key"* after the form was submitted empty and Moonraker answered 401. The app's message said only "HTTP 401"; it did not say whether a key had been sent, although the code has that information. The AI's own earlier "type it there" set its belief that a key had been typed.

5. *The key page without the port, then "the key isn't exposed that way".* The AI had just worked out that 8081 is Mainsail and 7125 is Moonraker. It searched, found Moonraker's documentation, which gives the key page as `http://{host}/access/api_key` with no port, and sent the person to `http://192.168.0.171/access/api_key`, port 80, a third server. When Chrome could not reach it, the AI concluded the key page does not exist on this printer, and in the same turn asked the app to try connecting again with nothing changed. The extra instructions explain how the app reaches Moonraker but never say that Moonraker's own web pages, the key page included, are at Moonraker's port too. I checked that the documentation omits the port.

6. *"Look for an API key or access page in Mainsail's settings"*, with no search. The extra instructions say: "You have not seen where Mainsail or Fluidd show the key, so search for where their version shows it before you say." That sentence assumes Mainsail shows the key somewhere. My own search found no such page: Mainsail's help page for this exact error says to add the computer's network to Moonraker's trusted-clients list instead. The AI filled in the assumption with a guess.

7. *The "send a report to the developers" card appeared after the second failure.* The app shows it at exactly the second failed attempt in a chat. Here the second failure was progress (Moonraker answered, the wrong-port problem was solved), but the rule only counts.

8. *"It's connected now, so you can send prints straight to it."* Klipper was in an error state. The standing instructions give this sentence as the example of how to finish after a successful check. The extra instructions say the check proves only that Moonraker answered. The app's message said only "verified"; the app had read Klipper's state from Moonraker and only logged it.

## Run 8. 4 November. Kenneth's real Raspberry Pi at `http://raspberrypi.local/`, no key needed, Klipper shut down. GPT-5.4 Mini. The person: "a generic Klipper printer, 240 × 225 bed, BLTouch". Connected in three turns.

1. *The AI asked the app to connect before any printer had been added*, got "add one first", and then asked "Which printer model is it?". Recovered in one turn.

2. *The same redundant "Want to connect it?"* as in run 7.

3. *"The field can be left blank or filled with the key from Mainsail's settings page."* Half right (blank), half the same unfounded assumption as run 7, with no search in this chat after the opening one.

4. *"It's connected, so you can send prints straight to it"* with Klipper shut down. Asked next "Is the printer ready to print right now?", the AI answered correctly: "I can't see the printer's current state from here, only that it's connected." It knew the fact from the extra instructions and said the standing instructions' sentence first.

5. *The bed size stayed 250 × 250* although the person said 240 × 225. While a printer is being added, the standing instructions say nothing about bed size and no action can set it. The AI dropped the fact without a word.

## Two things in this report I did not read myself

The no-printer case and the "Settings > LAN" case in run 4 come from the automated suite, and I have only the author's summary and the commit message for them. Everything else above I read in the transcript as the AI saw it.

+- **The printer chat**: the chat panel in JusPrin where a person adds a printer and can connect it. An AI model answers in it.
+- **The AI's standing instructions**: the text the AI reads at the start of every printer chat. It is written in the file `printerInstructions.ts`. I will call it "the standing instructions".

+- **The extra connection instructions**: a second text the app adds into the chat the first time the person tries to connect, chosen by the kind of connection (Bambu, Moonraker or OctoPrint). The code calls these files "skills"; I will say "the extra connection instructions". They begin with the sentence "The rules above still apply", so where the standing instructions and the extra instructions disagree, the standing instructions are meant to win.

+- **Actions the AI can ask the app to perform**: for connecting there are two. "Check connection status" (the code calls it `printer_connection_status`) asks the app what it knows about the printer on the network. "Connect" (`printer_connect`) asks the app to open a small form on screen where the person types the access code or API key, and then to try the connection. The AI never sees what is typed in that form.

+- **A message from the app**: a line the app itself writes into the chat for the AI to read, such as "Connection to Voron 2.4 350 failed: HTTP 401". The person did not type it and the AI did not write it.
+- **Bambu access code**: the six characters a Bambu printer shows on its own screen; a program must present them to connect over the local network.

+- **LAN Only mode**: a setting on a Bambu printer. When it is off, the printer talks to Bambu's cloud and JusPrin cannot connect to it. When it is on, JusPrin can connect directly. The code says "cloud mode" for off.

+- **The printer's broadcast**: a Bambu printer sends a small packet onto the local network about every ten seconds saying, in effect, "I am a P1S at this address, LAN Only on or off". The app finds Bambu printers by listening for these; nobody types an address.

+- **Bambu's network plug-in**: a closed-source library from Bambu that the app uses to talk to Bambu printers. When a connection fails it reports only a number, and the number was always -1 in these tests.

+- **Moonraker, Mainsail, Klipper**: Klipper is firmware that runs a hobbyist printer. Moonraker is the program beside it that other programs talk to over the network, normally on port 7125. Mainsail (or Fluidd) is the web page people open in a browser to use the printer; it talks to Moonraker for them.
+- **API key**: the long secret string Moonraker or OctoPrint can require from a program. Moonraker usually does not require one from a computer on the same home network.
+- **OctoPrint**: another program that runs beside a printer and offers a web page; it always requires an API key.

+- **The automated test program**: a program that starts the real JusPrin, opens the printer chat, and plays the person from a fixed list of lines ("say: Connect my printer", "type into the form: a wrong code"). I will say "the test program playing the person". It cannot react to what the AI says; it says its next line regardless.

+- **The AI models**: Claude Sonnet 5.5 from Anthropic (the stronger model used in most live runs); DeepSeek V4 Flash (a cheaper model used in the automated test suite); GPT-5.4 Mini from OpenAI (a cheaper model used on 4 November).

+- **Test printers in Docker**: on 3 and 4 November, Moonraker, Mainsail and OctoPrint were run as containers on Kenneth's Mac to stand in for real printers. They answer like the real programs but there is no printer behind them.

- **The standing instructions** are the text the AI reads at the start of every printer chat, written in the file `printerInstructions.ts`.

- **A message from the app** is a line the app itself writes into the chat for the AI to read, such as "Connection to Voron 2.4 350 failed: HTTP 401". The person did not type it and the AI did not write it.
- **Bambu access code**: the six characters a Bambu printer shows on its own screen; a program must present them to connect over the local network.
- **LAN Only mode**: a setting on a Bambu printer. When it is off, the printer talks to Bambu's cloud and JusPrin cannot connect to it. When it is on, JusPrin can connect directly.
- **The printer's broadcast**: a Bambu printer sends a small packet onto the local network about every ten seconds saying, in effect, "I am a P1S at this address, LAN Only on or off". The app finds Bambu printers by listening for these; nobody types an address.
- **Bambu's network plug-in**: a closed-source library from Bambu that the app uses to talk to Bambu printers. When a connection fails it reports only a number, and in these tests the number was always -1.
- **Klipper, Moonraker, Mainsail**: Klipper is firmware that runs a hobbyist printer. Moonraker is the program beside it that other programs talk to over the network, normally on port 7125. - **OctoPrint**: another program that runs beside a printer and offers a web page; it always requires an API key.
- **The test program playing the person**: a program that starts the real JusPrin, opens the printer chat, and plays the person from a fixed list of lines. It cannot react to what the AI says.

-Written 4 November 2026. This replaces an earlier version of the same file that used words of my own. Each run below is told as what happened, in order. For every failure I say what the AI had in front of it when it wrote the bad sentence, and what went wrong in that case alone. I draw no general conclusions here.

+Short version, 4 November. Words: the **standing instructions** are what the AI reads in every printer chat. The **extra connection instructions** are added by the app the first time the person tries to connect (the code calls them "skills"); they start with "The rules above still apply", so the standing instructions win a conflict. A **message from the app** is a line the app writes into the chat for the AI, such as "Connection to X failed: HTTP 401". **LAN Only** is the Bambu setting that must be on for JusPrin to connect. The **test program** plays the person from a fixed script and cannot react.
-## Words this report uses

+**Run 1, 31 Oct. Kenneth's P1S, LAN Only off, the shipped app.** The app said the plug-in was installed and "the printer can be connected", with no next step, so the AI asked for an address, which is the route for other printer kinds. Asked how to find it, the AI invented menu steps, because the standing instructions demand a location for every question. The app then refused with "no printer in LAN mode is on the network" before it had listened at all, and later hid the P1S it had heard with LAN Only off. The AI repeated the same three options three times, one of them a path the chat does not have, because the standing instructions forced them.
-- **The printer chat**: the chat panel in JusPrin where a person adds a printer and can connect it. An AI model answers in it.
-- **The AI's standing instructions**: the text the AI reads at the start of every printer chat. It is written in the file `printerInstructions.ts`. I will call it "the standing instructions".

-- **The extra connection instructions**: a second text the app adds into the chat the first time the person tries to connect, chosen by the kind of connection (Bambu, Moonraker or OctoPrint). The code calls these files "skills"; I will say "the extra connection instructions". They begin with the sentence "The rules above still apply", so where the standing instructions and the extra instructions disagree, the standing instructions are meant to win.

-- **Actions the AI can ask the app to perform**: for connecting there are two. "Check connection status" (the code calls it `printer_connection_status`) asks the app what it knows about the printer on the network. "Connect" (`printer_connect`) asks the app to open a small form on screen where the person types the access code or API key, and then to try the connection. The AI never sees what is typed in that form.

-- **A message from the app**: a line the app itself writes into the chat for the AI to read, such as "Connection to Voron 2.4 350 failed: HTTP 401". The person did not type it and the AI did not write it.
-- **Bambu access code**: the six characters a Bambu printer shows on its own screen; a program must present them to connect over the local network.

-- **LAN Only mode**: a setting on a Bambu printer. When it is off, the printer talks to Bambu's cloud and JusPrin cannot connect to it. When it is on, JusPrin can connect directly. The code says "cloud mode" for off.

-- **The printer's broadcast**: a Bambu printer sends a small packet onto the local network about every ten seconds saying, in effect, "I am a P1S at this address, LAN Only on or off". The app finds Bambu printers by listening for these; nobody types an address.

-- **Bambu's network plug-in**: a closed-source library from Bambu that the app uses to talk to Bambu printers. When a connection fails it reports only a number, and the number was always -1 in these tests.

-- **Moonraker, Mainsail, Klipper**: Klipper is firmware that runs a hobbyist printer. Moonraker is the program beside it that other programs talk to over the network, normally on port 7125. Mainsail (or Fluidd) is the web page people open in a browser to use the printer; it talks to Moonraker for them.
-- **API key**: the long secret string Moonraker or OctoPrint can require from a program. Moonraker usually does not require one from a computer on the same home network.
-- **OctoPrint**: another program that runs beside a printer and offers a web page; it always requires an API key.

-- **The automated test program**: a program that starts the real JusPrin, opens the printer chat, and plays the person from a fixed list of lines ("say: Connect my printer", "type into the form: a wrong code"). I will say "the test program playing the person". It cannot react to what the AI says; it says its next line regardless.

-- **The AI models**: Claude Sonnet 5.5 from Anthropic (the stronger model used in most live runs); DeepSeek V4 Flash (a cheaper model used in the automated test suite); GPT-5.4 Mini from OpenAI (a cheaper model used on 4 November).

-- **Test printers in Docker**: on 3 and 4 November, Moonraker, Mainsail and OctoPrint were run as containers on Kenneth's Mac to stand in for real printers. They answer like the real programs but there is no printer behind them.

+**Run 2, 1 Nov. Same P1S, app fixed to say what it heard, Sonnet.** Outcome right. The app then wrote into the chat: "Bambu's network plug-in is installed now, so Bambu Lab P1S can be connected." The AI replied: "Bambu Lab P1S can be connected now. I need the printer's address — the same one you open in a browser when you use it on your network." Kenneth asked how to find it; the AI said: "On the printer screen, tap the menu icon, then open Settings, then Network." Kenneth typed 192.168.0.198. The AI tried to connect and the app refused with "No printer in LAN mode is on the network now". The AI said: "It couldn't find the printer on the network right now. Try again with the same address, set up the connection manually in the app, or leave it for now." Kenneth said "try it again" and "try it now"; the AI gave the same three options twice more, once adding "after checking Bambu LAN mode on the printer". Kenneth never connected.

</built_in_browser>

<simulator_tools>
When the user wants to run, test, or visually check an iOS app ("run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?"), use mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control. Simulators and emulators only — when the user asks to run on their physical device ("on my phone", "on my device"), build for the device with your normal build tools instead; these tools and the panel cannot drive a real device. Open the live panel ('attach') whenever the user would want to see the app themselves — and call 'attach' FIRST, before you build or launch: it is cheap, it opens instantly on a booted device (and surfaces the one-time device-access prompt while the user is still at the keyboard), and if nothing is booted it returns a harmless, clear error — boot or build first in that case, then attach as soon as a device is up.
